	icchato+aniṣṭaprasaṅgam uktaṃ smārayati --- yasya tv iti/ vastupratyabhijñānāc ceti/ na
	hi devadattena dṛṣṭaṃ yajñadattaḥ pratyabhijānāti/ tasmād yaś cānubhavitā sa eva
	pratyabhijñāteti //3.14//
children.translated_text: become as large as the fruits of the palmyra palm. He concludes — 'Thus, everything — water, earth, and the rest — is constituted of all tastes and the rest.' He states the reason — 'Because of the non-destruction of the universal (<s>jāti</s>)' — since the universals of water-ness, earth-ness, and the like are recognized everywhere and hence are not destroyed. But if everything is constituted of everything, then — good heavens! — since everything would be present everywhere, at all times, and in all ways, the simultaneous manifestation of all entities would follow; for an effect whose complete cause is present surely cannot be delayed — to this he says: 'Place, time' etc. Although every cause is constituted of everything, nevertheless the place of a particular effect — for example, <s>Kāśmīra</s> is the place for saffron; even though [the causes] exist in <s>Pāñcāla</s> and other [regions], there is no operation [there], so saffron does not manifest in <s>Pāñcāla</s> etc. Similarly, in summer there is no operation of the rainy season, so there are no rice plants then. Similarly, a doe does not give birth to a human — there is no operation of human form in her. Similarly, one devoid of merit does not enjoy pleasure — there is no operation of the meritorious cause in him. Therefore, because of the non-conjunction — the departure — of place, time, form, and occasion, there is no simultaneous manifestation of the natures of entities. Having thus classified the <s>dharmas</s>, he shows the persistence of the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer) in them — 'That which in these' etc. The universal is the form of the <s>dharmin</s>; the particular is the <s>dharma</s>; [the <s>dharmin</s>] has both natures — this is the meaning. Having thus shown the persisting <s>dharmin</s>, he reminds [us] of the undesired consequence for the <s>Vaināśika</s> (Buddhist annihilationist) who does not accept it, [holding] consciousness to be momentary and mind-only — 'But for whom' etc. 'And because of the recognition of an entity' etc. For what was seen by <s>Devadatta</s> is not recognized by <s>Yajñadatta</s>. Therefore, the very one who experienced is the one who recognizes. (3.14)

He defines by a <s>sūtra</s> the <s>dharmin</s> in which this threefold transformation occurs — therein: 'The <s>dharmin</s> is that which follows the properties that are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminate.' Since a <s>dharmin</s> is that which possesses <s>dharma</s>, it cannot be known without knowing the <s>dharma</s>; therefore he shows the <s>dharma</s> — 'fitness' (<s>yogyatā</s>) etc. The capacity of the substance (<s>dharmin</s>) such as clay, etc. — the very capacity for producing powder, lump, pot, and the like — is the <s>dharma</s>; their existence there in unmanifest form — this is the meaning. But if they exist in unmanifest form, let them then become manifest from there. However, water-fetching and the like — not having been obtained from their own cause by those [pots, etc.] — from where have they come? Therefore it is said — 'delimited by fitness' etc. That capacity for the production of pots and the like, which is delimited by the fitness for water-fetching and the like — by that, water-fetching and the like are also obtained by pots and the like from their own cause alone; they are not causeless — this is the purport. Alternatively, [in answer to] 'what are the <s>dharmins</s>?' — the answer here is: 'those delimited by fitness are the <s>dharmins</s>.' [In answer to] 'what is <s>dharma</s>?' — the answer here is: capacity itself is <s>dharma</s>; their fitness itself is <s>dharma</s> — this is the meaning. Therefore, one that possesses that [<s>dharma</s>] is established as a <s>dharmin</s>. He states the evidence for the existence of that [<s>dharma</s>] — 'and that is inferred from the difference in the production of effects' — meaning: each <s>dharma</s> of a single <s>dharmin</s> has one form or another, such as powder, lump, pot, etc. And from seeing the difference in effects, [the <s>dharmas</s>] are distinct — this is the meaning. 'Observed' means 'apprehended.' Therein, he states the difference of the present clay-lump, which is subject to experience, from the quiescent and the indeterminate — from clay-powder and clay-pot — 'therein, the present' etc. If it were not differentiated, then like the lump, the powder and pot too would have the same operation and extension — this is the purport. But for the unmanifest [<s>dharma</s>] of the lump, the stated proof of difference is not applicable — thus he says — 'but when' etc. What is that [unmanifest dharma], and by what proof of difference is it differentiated?

children.text: kramānyatvaṃ pariṇāmānyatve hetuḥ //3.15//
children.translated_text: The difference in sequence (<s>krama</s>) is the cause of the difference in transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>). (3.15)

children.text:

	prāpteṣu viśiṣṭo+ayaṃ lakṣyata iti/
children.translated_text: there is only one transformation. For from a cause of a single nature, a difference of effects should not arise, since that would entail randomness — when this is established, [the reply] is stated: 'From the difference of sequence, the difference of transformation.' For a single lump of clay, the successive series of transformations — powder, lump, pot, potsherd, and particle — possessing sequence, is directly observed by ordinary examiners. And the succession of powder-to-lump is different from that of lump-to-pot, different from pot-to-potsherd, and different from potsherd-to-particle — because what is subsequent in one [stage] is prior in another. This difference of sequence, being operative within a single transformation, brings about a difference of transformation. And the single <s>dharmin</s> 'clay,' through the sequential arrival of successive cooperating conditions brought about by sequence, sustaining a successive series of transformations, does not make this [series] random — this is the purport. Just as the difference in sequence is the cause of difference in <s>dharma-pariṇāma</s> (property-transformation), so equally it is the cause of difference in <s>lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma</s> (character-transformation) and <s>avasthā-pariṇāma</s> (condition-transformation). This is elucidated by the <s>bhāṣya</s> — 'Of a single <s>dharmin</s>' etc. Taking the non-difference of sequence and the sequenced [thing], it is said 'that is its sequence.' Similarly for the sequence of condition-transformation. For thus — rice grains carefully preserved with effort by a farmer in a granary are observed, after very many years, to have their constituent structure disintegrating at the mere touch of the hand, undergoing the state of atoms. And this [disintegration] should not arise suddenly in what is fresh. Therefore, through the sequence of the series of moments, in the progressive order of subtle, subtler, subtlest, gross, grosser, grossest, and so on, this [change] is observed as having arrived at the distinct [stage].

	anumīyate/ evaṃ cetasaś ceṣṭā kriyā yathā yathā
children.translated_text: This difference of sequence exists only on the view that admits the distinction of <s>dharma</s> and <s>dharmin</s> — thus he says: 'These very' etc. From the modifications up to and including the <s>aliṅga</s> (the Unmanifest), the <s>dharma</s>-<s>dharmin</s> relation is relative — since even clay and the like are <s>dharmas</s> relative to the <s>tanmātras</s> — he says: 'Even a <s>dharma</s>' etc. When, through a figurative usage of non-difference applied to the ultimate <s>dharmin</s> — the <s>aliṅga</s> — and through that medium of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>), the <s>dharmin</s> itself is [treated as] <s>dharma</s> — to that extent. Then there is only a single transformation — a transformation of the <s>dharmin</s> itself — this is the meaning. Because the [categories of] property, character, and condition are absorbed into the essential nature of the <s>dharmin</s>. By this, the immutable eternality (<s>kūṭasthanityatva</s>) of the <s>dharmin</s> has been virtually refuted — as has been stated. While explaining <s>dharma-pariṇāma</s> (property-transformation), he incidentally states the varieties of <s>dharmas</s> of <s>citta</s> (mind) — 'Of <s>citta</s>' etc. '<s>Paridṛṣṭa</s>' means directly perceived; '<s>aparidṛṣṭa</s>' means beyond direct perception. Among those, the directly perceived [<s>dharmas</s>] are <s>pratyaya</s>-natured (cognitive) — <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) and the rest, <s>rāga</s> (passion) and the rest. '<s>Vastumātra</s>' (mere entities) indicates their non-luminous nature. One might think: if not directly perceived, then they simply do not exist — to this he says: 'Those whose existence is arrived at by inference, through mere entity[-ness] — they are so called.' Subsequently, due to the similarity with the mental, <s>āgama</s> (scriptural testimony) too is [a form of] inference. He collects the seven non-perceived [<s>dharmas</s>] in a verse — '<s>Nirodha</s>' etc. <s>Nirodha</s> (cessation) — the state of <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive absorption) of the <s>cittavṛttis</s> (mental modifications), the state of being a mere residue of <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) — is ascertained from scripture and from inference. By the word '<s>dharma</s>' he indicates merit and demerit. In some readings the word is '<s>karma</s>'; even there, the merit and demerit produced by it are what is intended. Those are known from scripture and by inference from the observation of the experience of pleasure and pain. <s>Saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) is inferred from memory. Similarly, since <s>citta</s> has the three <s>guṇas</s>, and the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is fluctuating, moment-by-moment transformation is inferred. Similarly, <s>jīvana</s> (vitality) — the maintenance of <s>prāṇa</s> (life-force) — a variety of effort that is an unperceived <s>dharma</s> of <s>citta</s>, is inferred from inhalation and exhalation. Similarly, the activity (<s>ceṣṭā</s>) of the mind — action — according as

children.translated_text: From <s>saṃyama</s> (perfect discipline) on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and future [arises]. (3.16)

children.text:
ataḥ param ā pādaparisamāpteḥ saṃyamaviṣayas tadvaśīkārasūcanī vibhūtiś ca vaktavyā/

	sākṣātkārayed ity ata āha --- tena pariṇāmatrayaṃ sākṣātkriyamāṇaṃ teṣu pariṇāmeṣv
	anugate ye atītānāgate tadviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ saṃpādayati/ pariṇāmatrayasākṣātkaraṇam eva
	tadantarbhūtātītānāgatasākṣātkaraṇātmakam iti na viṣayabhedaḥ saṃyamasākṣātkārayor ity
	arthaḥ //3.16//
children.translated_text: Henceforth, up to the end of the chapter, the objects of <s>saṃyama</s> and the <s>vibhūtis</s> (supernatural powers) that indicate mastery over them are to be stated. Therein, the threefold transformation (<s>pariṇāmatraya</s>) of the kind already described is first introduced as the object of <s>saṃyama</s> for the <s>yogin</s> who has undertaken all the limbs of <s>yoga</s> — 'From <s>saṃyama</s> on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and future.' Now, [one might object:] where <s>saṃyama</s> is applied, there alone does direct realization occur; how then would <s>saṃyama</s> on the three transformations bring about the direct realization of the past and future? Hence he says — 'by that, when the three transformations are directly realized, [the yogin] produces knowledge concerning the past and future that inhere in those transformations.' The direct realization of the three transformations is itself constituted by the direct realization of the past and future contained within them — thus there is no difference of object between <s>saṃyama</s> and direct realization — such is the meaning. (3.16)

children.translated_text: Due to the mutual superimposition of word (<s>śabda</s>), meaning (<s>artha</s>), and cognition (<s>pratyaya</s>), there is their conflation. From <s>saṃyama</s> on their differentiation, [arises] knowledge of the sounds of all beings. (3.17)

children.translated_text: Here another object of <s>saṃyama</s> is introduced — 'Due to the mutual superimposition of word, meaning, and cognition, there is their conflation. From <s>saṃyama</s> on their differentiation, knowledge of the sounds of all beings.' Here, intending to explain the signifying word (<s>śabda</s>), he first states the object of the operation of speech — 'therein, speech (<s>vāc</s>), the organ of speech, is that which manifests the phonemes (<s>varṇas</s>), having eight places [of articulation].' As it is said —

children.translated_text: having the form of phonemes — [the ear] is transformed with that form and has <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle elements) as its object, not the signifier — such is the meaning. He distinguishes the signifier from the phonemes established in common usage — 'but the word (<s>pada</s>) is the signifier, graspable by the synthetic cognition that combines the sounds (<s>nāda</s>).' Having individually grasped the sounds, the phonemes, as established in common experience, [the cognition] that subsequently combines them, bringing them to unity — 'go [cow]' is this single word — by that [synthetic cognition] the word is grasped. Although the earlier cognitions too apprehend the word in the form of each phoneme individually, nevertheless [the word] does not shine forth distinctly. But in the final cognition, it [shines forth] most distinctly — hence it is said to be 'graspable by the synthetic cognition that combines sounds.' Now, to one who, due to [perceiving] dissimilarity, fails to recognize the experience of a single word and maintains that the phonemes themselves are the signifiers, he replies — 'the phonemes,' etc. Could these phonemes individually produce a cognition directed toward the signified, either like pegs [each independently supporting] a swing's hanging, or like stones combined [together supporting] a pot? The first option is not [possible] — because cognition of meaning does not arise from a single [phoneme], or if it did, there would be no need to pronounce the second and subsequent [phonemes], since an instrument that has already accomplished its purpose would be imposing [further] specifications on the action — which would violate the principle of instrumental causation. Therefore, the second [option] remains. Now, it is possible for combined stones to support a pot because they exist simultaneously. But the simultaneous existence of phonemes is impossible; therefore, since they cannot serve as mutual auxiliaries, even combined they do not produce a cognition of meaning. Those [phonemes], not touching the single reality of the word (<s>pada</s>) by identity with it, and hence not bringing it to presentation — [they are] like iron bars, manifest and then vanished, each individually not having the nature of a word — thus they are described. But if the phonemes were to touch the single word by identity, then the stated defects would not arise — hence he says: 'each single phoneme is of the nature of the word, endowed with all expressive powers' — packed with all the powers of expression. For the phoneme 'g' is seen in expressions like <s>go</s> (cow), <s>gaṇa</s> (group), <s>gaura</s> (white), <s>naga</s> (mountain), and the like, which express meanings like cow-ness and so on — hence it possesses the respective expressive powers. Likewise, the vowel 'o' is seen in words like <s>soma</s>, <s>śocis</s> (flame), and the like, which express meanings like <s>Īśvara</s> (Lord) and so on — hence it too possesses the respective expressive powers. The same should be understood throughout. And each individual phoneme such as 'g' and the like — that other phoneme such as 'o' and the like which is its co-occurring auxiliary is its very correlate, its counter-correlate; the state of being such is its reality. From that [reality arises] a diversity-like-appearance (<s>vaiśvarūpya</s>), but [the phoneme] has not [actually] become diverse — because of its [unified] reality. Thus the prior phoneme 'g,' being distinguished from words like <s>gaṇa</s> and the like by the subsequent 'o,' and the subsequent 'o' being distinguished from words like <s>śocis</s> and the like by 'g,'

children.translated_text: is established in the specific <s>sphoṭa</s> (meaning-bearing linguistic unit) of the word <s>go</s>, which signifies cow-ness, in the synthetic cognition. This is the purport: the cognition of meaning cannot be produced by phonemes that have a fixed sequence and cannot exist simultaneously. Nor is the aggregation of phonemes — even though they may lack fixed sequence, like the [ritual actions] <s>agneya</s> and the like in producing an unprecedented [result] such as <s>apūrva</s> or heaven — applicable to the generation of meaning-cognition, because such a hypothesis cannot withstand scrutiny at present. Now, this <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) generated by the experience of phonemes, which is the cause of the production of memory — [some claim it is] a different [thing] called <s>apūrva</s>, like [the saṃskāra] generated by <s>agneya</s> and the like. But that [hypothesis] first of all [fails because] — the immediately following [option] would lead to excessive complexity of postulation. That very [saṃskāra], being of an unprecedented kind, would have to be postulated, and since the production of a single [saṃskāra] from sequential phoneme-experiences is not possible, one would have to postulate multiple intermediate <s>saṃskāras</s> of the same kind — hence [this is] cumbersome. Nor does this [saṃskāra], being unknown, serve as a component of the evidencing ground — for an unknown [entity] cannot take on the role of a component. Surely an unknown relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>) cannot serve as a component of conveying meaning. And a <s>saṃskāra</s> inferred from the production of memory as its result is restricted to the object of the experience that is its cause and cannot produce cognition regarding a different object — otherwise, having experienced any single thing, everyone would know everything. Nor is it tenable that phonemes, having attained co-existence through the mirror of memory born from the aggregate of <s>saṃskāras</s> generated by the experience of individual phonemes, and [thereby] having their co-presence apprehended, become signifiers — because phonemes experienced in [correct] sequence, in the wrong sequence, or randomly would all equally produce meaning-cognition [under that hypothesis], without any distinction. Nor can this memory-knowledge apprehend the relation of precedence and subsequence that belongs to the prior experience. Therefore, the cognition of meaning, being impossible from phonemes [alone], requires as its cause nothing other than the experience of the single word (<s>pada</s>). Nor does this [difficulty] apply to the word [itself]. For the sounds (<s>dhvanis</s>), which individually manifest [the word] through different articulatory efforts, being similar [to each other] as they are produced with the same place and manner of articulation as the mutually dissimilar sounds that manifest their respective words — they make the single word appear as though it had parts and as though it were manifold through the imposition of similarity to different correlate words, since the similarities differ according to different correlates. Just as the face, which is single with its fixed color, size, and shape, is reflected by gems, swords, mirrors, and the like as having different colors, sizes, and shapes and as being manifold — but not in reality. The phonemes are merely parts imputed through the imposition of different similarities to the partless word. Therefore, the cognition of phonemes takes as its object the <s>sphoṭa</s> (meaning-bearing unit) of the word in its undivided nature, though it appears as if divided and as if having parts. Thus, the 'g'-portion of the single <s>sphoṭa</s> of the word <s>go</s>, by its similarity to the <s>sphoṭas</s> of words like <s>gaura</s> (white) and the like, cannot by itself determine its own host [sphoṭa]; therefore, qualified by 'o,' it does determine [it]. Likewise, the 'o'-portion, being similar to the words <s>śocis</s> and the like, is unable by itself to determine its host, the <s>sphoṭa</s> of the word <s>go</s>; therefore, qualified by 'g,' it determines [it]. And even for [phonemes] that do not co-exist, there can be co-existence through the medium of <s>saṃskāras</s> — hence the relationship of qualifier and qualified is justified. Nor is there a difference of object between the two <s>saṃskāras</s>, since the experiences directed at the two parts and the <s>saṃskāras</s> born from them both have a single word as their object. children.translated_text: The word (<s>pada</s>) is experienced as unmanifest; through the synthesizing cognition (<s>anusaṃhāra-dhī</s>), born from the <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) generated by the experience of parts, it becomes manifest — such is the distinction. Prior, unmanifest experiences, depositing <s>saṃskāras</s> in sequence, have been observed to produce a manifest experience — just as from a distance, the unmanifest cognitions 'there is something' regarding a tree produce the manifest cognition of a tree. But this procedure is not possible for individual letters (<s>varṇas</s>) in conveying meaning. It cannot be said that letters individually deposit unmanifest meaning-cognitions and at the end produce a manifest one — since the manifest/unmanifest character is restricted to perceptual cognition alone. The meaning-cognition deposited by letters, however, is not perceptual; therefore, arising from letters, it would either arise clearly, or not arise at all — but not unclearly. But for the <s>sphoṭa</s> (the integral sound-unit), which is manifested by sound (<s>dhvani</s>) and is perceptual, the clear and unclear states are posited — hence [the cases are] not analogous. Thus, in the synthesizing cognition born from the ear-perception aided by the <s>saṃskāras</s> generated from the experience of individual letters, the letters combined, having assumed the nature of a single word-<s>sphoṭa</s>, being manifested by a particular effort, and since that particular effort depends on a fixed sequence — if the sequence were different, there would be absence of that particular manifesting effort and hence absence of that manifestation — [the letters], conforming to the sequence and delimited by a meaning-convention, show only the worldly convention-delimitation regarding similar words: 'These many — two or three, three or four, five or six — these [letters] <s>ga-kāra</s>, <s>au-kāra</s>, <s>visarjanīya</s>, endowed with the capacity to designate all [meanings], illuminate the meaning possessing dewlap (<s>sāsnā</s>) and the like.' Then, is it that by following convention, the letters alone have designating capacity, and hence there is no single entity called a 'word'? Hence he says — 'of these,' etc. A sequence whose cause is sounds is a 'sound-sequence' (<s>dhvanikrama</s>); those in whom the sound-sequence has been synthesized are so called. '<s>Buddhinirbhāsa</s>' means illuminated, manifested by intellect. 'Delimited by convention' — in conformity with the understanding of the gross-seeing public, it has been stated as '<s>ga-kāra</s>, <s>au-kāra</s>, <s>visarjanīya</s>.' Since the <s>ga-kāra</s> and the rest too have designating capacity through being parts [of the word] and through identity [with it], but following actual cognition, a single word alone is the designator — such is the meaning. He clarifies this — 'that single word is cognized through worldly cognition' — such is the connection. Why single? Hence he says — 'the object of a single cognition: "cow" is a single word' — since it is the object of a cognition of a single form, therefore it is single. He states its manifester — 'produced by a single effort,' etc. The effort that manifests the word '<s>rasa</s>' is different from the effort that manifests the word '<s>sara</s>.' And the latter, from its beginning, delimited by the fruit characterized as the manifestation of the word '<s>sara</s>,' being progressive [i.e., sequential], is single. That [word] produced by it is without parts — since the parts, assumed through imposed similarity-distinctions, do not ultimately exist. Hence, being of progressive nature, it is without sequence. [Objection:] But the letters are sequential, and they are its parts — so how can it be without sequence and without parts? Hence he says — 'without letters' (<s>avarṇa</s>). For the letters are not its parts; rather, through the imposed distinctions of similarity,

For the reflections in gems, swords, mirrors, and the like are not truly parts of the [reflected] face. The Buddhist [view]: in the synthesizing cognition, what is recognized is the activity of the final-letter cognition — [namely] the <s>saṃskāra</s>, combined with the <s>saṃskāras</s> generated by the experience of prior letters — by which [the meaning] has been presented, made into an object. The fact that letter-experiences and their respective <s>saṃskāras</s> have the word as their object has been established above. [Objection:] If the word-reality (<s>padatattva</s>) is without parts, without sequence, and without letters, why does it sometimes not manifest as such? For a crystal gem whose redness has been produced by the application of lac-juice is not experienced as clear and white upon the removal of that [lac] — therefore the letters are ultimately real. Hence he says — 'elsewhere,' etc. With the intention of establishing [this], the words that are being pronounced and heard by hearers — this beginningless convention of speech (<s>vāgvyavahāra</s>), dependent on the connection of distinct letters and words — the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) generated by it is also beginningless. Just as lac and the like [serve as <s>upādhis</s>] — upon its removal, the crystal shines with its natural clear white color — that is appropriate. But the cognition of a word, since it never arises from anything other than the distinction of sounds brought about by the distinction of effort, and since [that sound-distinction] is always tainted by the fault of similarity and hence always generates cognition in the form of letters alone — whence would there be a manifestation of the word without a limiting adjunct? children.translated_text: He whose nature is such is so described. For it is not merely that the convention as established determines the meaning, but rather [the convention] as it is being remembered. This amounts to saying: in the convention, which is of undifferentiated form, having conceptually superimposed some distinction, the genitive case is employed. He who knows the differentiation among these, when he performs <s>saṃyama</s> (meditative constraint) thereon, becomes omniscient, a knower of the cries of all beings. Thus, having derived the word — which is one and partless — with its conceptually divided letter-parts, in order to derive the sentence — which is one and partless — with its conceptually divided word-parts, he says: "In all words there exists sentence-potency (<s>vākyaśakti</s>)." The intention is this: speech (<s>śabda</s>) is employed for communicating to another, and what is to be communicated to the other is precisely what is intended by the speakers; and what is intended by them is that which pertains to the domain of material cause and the rest. And it is not mere word-meaning that is its domain, but rather sentence-meaning — thus all words are directed toward sentence-meaning, and that alone is their meaning. Therefore, even where a single word is used independently, its meaning is understood only by combining it with another word, and not from the word alone — why? Because of the incapacity of that [word] by itself. And so in each case it is the sentence alone that is the signifier, not the individual words. But as parts of that [sentence], they too have the capacity to signify sentence-meaning, just as letters, as parts of a word, [signify] word-meaning. Therefore, just as each letter is endowed with the capacity to signify all word-meanings, so too each word is endowed with the capacity to signify all sentence-meanings. This is what is stated: "In all words there exists sentence-potency" — when "tree" (<s>vṛkṣa</s>) is uttered, "exists" is understood. The word <s>vṛkṣa</s>, combined with the supplied word "exists" (<s>asti</s>), functions in the sentence-meaning — and because it is a part of that [sentence], the word <s>vṛkṣa</s> functions therein. As to why "exists" is understood, he says: "Word-meaning does not deviate from existence (<s>sattā</s>)." For common usage alone is the means of ascertaining the meanings of words. And common usage, by combining the mere word-meaning with the meaning of existence, everywhere produces a sentence-meaning — this is the invariable association of word-meaning with existence. Hence the practice of those who know linguistic usage: where no other verb is present, <s>asti</s> or <s>bhavanti</s> and the like are to be supplied. Having stated that the nominal stem (<s>prātipadika</s>) is invariably associated with undifferentiated action, he shows that action is invariably associated with case-relations (<s>kāraka</s>) — thus [the <s>sūtra</s>] says "and when <s>pacati</s> (he cooks) is uttered." For when <s>pacati</s> is uttered, a mere <s>kāraka</s> suitable for syntactic connection with it is understood,

	sphuṭataro hy atra pūrvāparībhūtāyāḥ kriyāyāḥ sādhyarūpāyāḥ siddharūpaḥ kriyārthaḥ
	śvetata iti bhinnaḥ śabdaḥ/ yatrāpi śabdārthayoḥ siddharūpatvaṃ tatrāpy arthād asti
	śabdasya bheda ity āha --- śvetaḥ prāsāda iti kārakārthaḥ śabdaḥ/ abhihitatvāc ca
	kārakavibhakter abhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: moreover, since a word is seen to function in the sentence-meaning, all the more so do words possess sentence-potency (<s>vākyaśakti</s>) — thus he says "and it is observed" (<s>dṛṣṭaṃ ca</s>). But even so, an independent word like <s>śrotriya</s> and the rest does not convey meaning of this kind until it is combined with [verbs like] <s>asti</s> and the rest. And thus, since even this [word] is a part of a sentence, its [independence] is merely conceptual — this is the purport. One might object: if words themselves have sentence-potency, then what need is there for the sentence, since the sentence-meaning would be determined from them alone? To this he says "therein the sentence..." (<s>tatra vākya</s>). This has been stated: the intended word-meaning is not understood from a word alone until it is combined with another word.

children.text:
arthaṃ vibhajate --- kriyākārakātmā tadarthas
	tayoḥ śabdayor arthaḥ kriyātmā kārakātmā ca/ pratyayaṃ vibhajate --- pratyayaś ceti/
	caśabdena tadartha ity etat padam atrānukṛṣyate/ tad atrānyapadārthapradhānaṃ
	saṃbadhyate/ sa eva kriyākārakātmārtho yasya sa tathoktaḥ/ nanv abhedena pratīteḥ
	śabdārthapratyayānāṃ saṃkarāt kutaḥ pravibhāga ity āśayavān pṛcchati --- kasmād iti/
	uttaram āha --- so+ayam ity abhisaṃbandhād iti/ saṃketopādhir ekākārapratyayo na tu
	tāttvika ity arthaḥ/ saṃketasya nimittatā darśitā saṃketa iti saptamyā/ paramārtham āha
	--- yas tu śveto+artha iti/ avasthā navapurāṇatvādayaḥ/ sahagataḥ saṃkīrṇaḥ/ evaṃ ca
	pravibhāgasaṃyamād yoginaḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ paśumṛgasarīsṛpavayaḥprabhṛtīnāṃ yāni
	rutāni tatrāpy avyaktaṃ padaṃ tadarthas tatpratyayaś ceti/ tad iha
	manuṣyavacanavācyapratyayeṣu kṛtaḥ saṃyamaḥ samānajātīyatayā teṣv api kṛta eveti/ teṣāṃ
	rutaṃ tadarthabhedaṃ tatpratyayaṃ ca yogī jānātīti siddham //3.17//
children.translated_text: He analyzes the meaning: "the meaning thereof is of the nature of action (<s>kriyā</s>) and case-relation (<s>kāraka</s>)" — the meaning of those two words is of the nature of action and of the nature of case-relation. He analyzes the cognition: "and the cognition" (<s>pratyayaś ca</s>) — by the word "ca" (and), the phrase "the meaning thereof" (<s>tadartha</s>) is drawn into this [clause]. Therein, what is primarily the meaning of another word is connected. That very meaning which is of the nature of action and case-relation — he whose [cognition has that character] is so described. But since they are cognized without distinction, from the confusion of word (<s>śabda</s>), meaning (<s>artha</s>), and cognition (<s>pratyaya</s>), whence the differentiation? — with this intent, he asks "why?" (<s>kasmāt</s>). He gives the answer: "because of the correlation indicated by 'this is that'" — the cognition of uniform appearance is conditioned by convention (<s>saṃketa</s>), and is not real — this is the meaning. The nature of convention...

Since the word-reality (<s>padātman</s>) manifests as tinged with distinct letters, therefore the gross-seeing public, considering the letters alone to be the word, conventionalizes those very [letters] as bearing variety-distinctions in the distinction of meanings — hence he says — 'of that,' etc. Of that single word, even for one who does not know [its true nature], for the benefit of the gross-seeing public, the division by letter-nature [is made] from the cognition of convention. He states the division — 'Of this many — neither fewer nor more — of such a kind, a particular sequence without interruption, a synthesis, a grasping by a single cognition, is the designator of one meaning such as <s>gotva</s> (cowhood)' — thus. [Objection:] If this word is the designator of a single meaning — such is the convention — then, sir, there should be no mutual superimposition of word and meaning! Hence he says — 'But the convention,' etc. 'In memory, the self —'

children.text: saṃskārasākṣātkaraṇāt pūrvajātijñānam //3.18//
children.translated_text: From direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions), knowledge of previous births [arises]. (3.18)

children.text:
saṃskārasākṣātkaraṇāt pūrvajātijñānam/ jñānajā hi saṃskārāḥ smṛter
	hetavo+avidyādisaṃskārā avidyādīnāṃ kleśānāṃ hetavaḥ/ vipāko jātyāyurbhogarūpas tasya
	hetavo dharmādharmarūpāḥ/ pūrveṣu bhaveṣv abhisaṃskṛtā niṣpāditāḥ svakāraṇair
	yathāsaṃskṛtaṃ vyañjanaṃ kṛtam iti gamyate/ pariṇāmaceṣṭānirodhaśaktijīvanāny eva
	dharmāś cittasya tadvad aparidṛṣṭāś cittadharmās teṣu śruteṣv anumiteṣu

saparikareṣu saṃyamaḥ saṃskārāṇāṃ dvayeṣāṃ sākṣātkriyāyai samarthaḥ/ astu tatra saṃyamāt
	tatsākṣātkāraḥ pūrvajātisākṣātkāras tu kuta ity ata āha --- na ca deśeti/ nimittaṃ
	pūrvaśarīram indriyādi ca/ sānubandhasaṃskārasākṣātkāra eva nāntarīyakatayā
	jātyādisākṣātkāram ākṣipatīty arthaḥ/ svasaṃskārasaṃyamaṃ parakīyeṣv atidiśati ---
	paratrāpy evam iti/ atra śraddhotpāde hetum anubhavata āvaṭyasya jaigīṣavyeṇa saṃvādam
	upanyasyati --- atredam ākhyānaṃ śrūyata iti/ mahākalpo mahāsargaḥ/ tanudhara iti
	nirmāṇakāyasaṃpad uktā/ bhavyaḥ śobhano vigalitarajastamomala ity arthaḥ/
	pradhānavaśitvam aiśvaryaṃ tena hi pradhānaṃ vikṣobhya yasmai yādṛśīṃ kāyendriyasaṃpadaṃ
	ditsati tasmai tādṛśīṃ datte/ svakīyāni ca kāyendriyasahasrāṇi nirmāyāntarikṣe divi
	bhuvi ca yathecchaṃ viharatīti/ saṃtoṣo hi tṛṣṇākṣayo buddhisattvasya praśāntatā
	dharmaḥ //3.18//
children.translated_text: <s>saṃyama</s> (meditative constraint) on [these <s>saṃskāras</s>] together with their accompaniments is capable of directly perceiving both types of <s>saṃskāras</s>. Granted that from <s>saṃyama</s> thereon comes direct perception of those [<s>saṃskāras</s>], but whence the direct perception of past lives? To this he says "not place..." (<s>na ca deśa</s>). The cause is the former body, sense-organs, and the rest. The direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s> together with their connections necessarily entails the direct perception of birth and the rest — this is the meaning. He extends [the application of] <s>saṃyama</s> on one's own <s>saṃskāras</s> to those of others: "in others too, similarly" (<s>paratrāpy evam</s>). Here, to generate faith through experience, he presents the dialogue of <s>Āvaṭya</s> with <s>Jaigīṣavya</s>: "Herein this narrative is heard." A great <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic cycle) means a great creation. The embodied one...

From direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s>, knowledge of previous births. For <s>saṃskāras</s> born of knowledge are the causes of memory, while <s>saṃskāras</s> of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the rest are the causes of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) such as <s>avidyā</s> and the rest. Fruition (<s>vipāka</s>) takes the form of birth (<s>jāti</s>), lifespan (<s>āyus</s>), and experience (<s>bhoga</s>); its causes are of the form of merit (<s>dharma</s>) and demerit (<s>adharma</s>). [These <s>saṃskāras</s> were] fashioned and produced by their own causes in previous existences, just as a prepared condiment is understood to have been made [from its ingredients]. Transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), activity (<s>ceṣṭā</s>), cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), potency (<s>śakti</s>), and vitality (<s>jīvana</s>) are indeed the properties of the mind; similarly, there are imperceptible mental properties — when these are heard of or inferred,

children.text: pratyayasya paracittajñānam //3.19//
children.translated_text: From [<s>saṃyama</s> on] the cognition [of another], knowledge of others' minds [arises]. (3.19)

children.text: pratyayasya paracittajñānam/ parapratyayasya cittamātrasya sākṣātkaraṇād iti //3.19//
children.translated_text: From [<s>saṃyama</s> on] the cognition, knowledge of others' minds — from direct perception of another's cognition, of the mind alone. (3.19)

children.text: na ca tat sālambanaṃ tasyāviṣayībhūtatvāt //3.20//
children.translated_text: But that [knowledge] does not include the support [i.e., the object of the other's mind], because that [object] has not become the object [of the yogin's perception]. (3.20)

children.text:
yathā saṃskārasākṣātkāras tadanubandhapūrvajanmasākṣātkāram ākṣipaty evaṃ
	paracittasākṣātkāro+api tadālambanasākṣātkāram ākṣiped iti prāpta āha --- na ca tat
	sālambanaṃ tasyāviṣayībhūtatvāt/ sānubandhasaṃskāraviṣayo 'sau saṃyamo+ayaṃ tu
	paracittamātraviṣaya ity abhiprāyaḥ //3.20//
children.translated_text: Just as the direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) entails the direct perception of previous births connected with them, so too the direct perception of another's mind might entail the direct perception of the objects [of that mind] — anticipating this, he says — 'but that [knowledge] is not accompanied by the object (<s>sālambana</s>), because [the object] has not become the domain [of this saṃyama].' The intention is: that [former] <s>saṃyama</s> has as its object the <s>saṃskāras</s> together with their connections, whereas this [present saṃyama] has as its object merely the other's mind. (3.20)

children.text: kāyarūpasaṃyamāt tadgrāhyaśaktistambhe cakṣuṣprakāśāsaṃprayoge+antardhānam //3.21//
children.translated_text: Through <s>saṃyama</s> (perfect discipline) on the form of the body, when the power of being perceived is arrested, and [there is] disconnection from the light of the eye — invisibility (<s>antardhāna</s>). (3.21)

children.text:
kāyarūpasaṃyamāt tadgrāhyaśaktistambhe cakṣuṣprakāśasaṃprayoge+antardhānam/ pañcātmakaḥ
	kāyaḥ/ sa ca rūpavattayā cākṣuṣo bhavati/ rūpeṇa hi kāyaś ca tadrūpaṃ ca
	cakṣurgrahaṇakarmaśaktim anubhavati/ tatra yadā rūpe saṃyamaviśeṣo yoginā kriyate tadā
	rūpasya grāhyaśaktī rūpavatkāyapratyakṣatāhetuḥ stambhyate/ tasmād grāhyaśaktistambhe
	saty antardhānaṃ yoginas tataḥ parakīyacakṣurjanitena prakāśena jñānenāsaṃprayogaś
	cakṣurjñānāviṣayatvaṃ yoginaḥ kāyasyeti yāvat/ tasmin kartavye+antardhānaṃ kāraṇam ity
	arthaḥ/ eteneti/ kāyaśabdasparśarasagandhasaṃyamāt tadgrāhyaśaktistambhe
	śrotratvagrasanaghrāṇaprakāśāsaṃprayoge+antardhānam iti sūtram ūhanīyam //3.21//
children.translated_text: Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the form of the body, when the power of being perceived is arrested, and there is disconnection from the light of the eye — invisibility. The body is composed of five [elements]. And by virtue of having form (<s>rūpa</s>), it becomes an object of the eye. For the body, through its form, and that form [itself], undergo the operative power of being grasped by the eye. Therein, when a special <s>saṃyama</s> is performed by the <s>yogin</s> on the form, the power of being perceived — the cause of the body with form being directly perceptible — is arrested. Therefore, when the power of being perceived is arrested, there is invisibility of the <s>yogin</s>; consequently, there is disconnection from the knowledge — the illumination — generated by another's eye, meaning the <s>yogin</s>'s body becomes imperceptible to visual cognition. Invisibility is the cause of what is to be accomplished — this is the meaning. 'By this' etc. — from <s>saṃyama</s> on the body's sound, touch, taste, and smell, when the power of being perceived is arrested, and there is disconnection from the illumination of ear, skin, tongue, and nose — invisibility: this <s>sūtra</s> should be inferred [by extension]. (3.21)

children.text: sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamād aparāntajñānam ariṣṭebhyo vā //3.22//
children.translated_text: <s>Karma</s> (action) is of two kinds — with onset (<s>sopakrama</s>) and without onset (<s>nirupakrama</s>). Through <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of the time of death (<s>aparānta</s>) [arises]; or from portents (<s>ariṣṭa</s>). (3.22)

children.text:
sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma tatsaṃyamād aparāntajñānam ariṣṭebhyo vā/ āyurvipākaṃ
	ca karma dvividhaṃ sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca/ yat khalv aikabhavikaṃ karma
	jātyāyurbhogahetus tad āyurvipākam/ tac ca kiṃcitkālānapekṣam eva bhogadānāya prasthitaṃ
	dattabahubhogam alpāvaśiṣṭaphalaṃ pravṛttavyāpāraṃ kevalaṃ tatphalasya sahasā bhoktum
	ekena śarīreṇāśakyatvād vilambate tad idaṃ sopakramam/ upakramo vyāpāras tatsahitam ity
	arthaḥ/ tad eva tu dattastokaphalaṃ tatkālam apekṣya phaladānāya vyāpriyamāṇaṃ
	kādācitkamandavyāpāraṃ nirupakramam/ etad eva nidarśanābhyāṃ viśadayati --- tatra
	yatheti/ atraivātivaiśadyāya nidarśanāntaraṃ darśayati --- yathā vāgnir iti/ parāntaṃ
	mahāpralayam apekṣyāparānto maraṇam/ tasmin karmaṇi dharmādharmayoḥ saṃyamād
	aparāntajñānam/ tataś ca yogī sopakramam ātmanaḥ karma vijñāya bahūn kāyān nirmāya
	sahasā phalaṃ bhuktvā svecchayā mriyate/ prāsaṅgikam āha --- ariṣṭebhyo vā/ arivat
	trāsayantīty ariṣṭāni trividhāni maraṇacihnāni/ viparītaṃ vā sarvaṃ
	māhendrajālādivyatirekeṇa grāmanagarādi svargam abhimanyate, manuṣyalokam eva devalokam
	iti //3.22//
children.translated_text: <s>Karma</s> is of two kinds — with onset and without onset. Through <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of death; or from portents. The <s>karma</s> whose fruition is lifespan is also of two kinds: with onset (<s>sopakrama</s>) and without onset (<s>nirupakrama</s>). That <s>karma</s> which pertains to a single birth and is the cause of class of birth, lifespan, and experience — that is <s>karma</s> whose fruition is lifespan. And some of that, without waiting for [a particular] time, has proceeded to give experience, has given much of its fruit, has little remaining fruit, and has commenced its operation — but merely because its fruit cannot be experienced suddenly in a single body, it is delayed. This is '<s>sopakrama</s>' (with onset). 'Onset' means operation; 'accompanied by that' is the meaning. That same [<s>karma</s>], however, which has given little fruit and, awaiting the right time to give its fruit, operates only occasionally and feebly — that is '<s>nirupakrama</s>' (without onset). He clarifies this with two illustrations — 'therein, just as' etc. For even greater clarity, he shows another illustration — 'just as fire' etc. <s>Parānta</s> refers to the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>); relative to that, <s>aparānta</s> means death. Through <s>saṃyama</s> on that <s>karma</s> — on <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> — comes knowledge of death. And thereby the <s>yogin</s>, having discerned his own <s>karma</s> as being with onset, creates many bodies, quickly experiences the fruit, and dies at will. He states what is incidental — 'or from portents.' <s>Ariṣṭas</s> — so called because they frighten like an enemy — are the threefold signs of death. Or, everything is perceived in a reversed manner — apart from magic and the like — one regards villages, cities, and the like as heaven, the human world itself as the divine world. (3.22)

children.text: maitryādiṣu balāni //3.23//
children.translated_text: [Through <s>saṃyama</s>] on friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>) and the rest, [come] strengths (<s>bala</s>). (3.23)

children.text:
maitryādiṣu balāni/ maitryādiṣu saṃyamān maitryādibalāny asya bhavanti/ tatra
	maitrībhāvanāto balaṃ yena jīvalokaṃ sukhākaroti tataḥ sarvahito bhavati/ evaṃ
	karuṇābalāt prāṇino duḥkhād duḥkhahetor vā samuddharati/ evaṃ muditābalāj jīvalokasya
	mādhyasthyam ādhatte/ vakṣyamāṇaupayikaṃ bhāvanākāraṇatvaṃ samādher āha --- bhāvanātaḥ
	samādhir yaḥ sa saṃyamaḥ/ yady api dhāraṇādhyānasamādhitrayam eva saṃyamo na
	samādhimātraṃ tathāpi samādhyanantaraṃ kāryotpādāt samādheḥ prādhānyāt tatra saṃyama
	upacaritaḥ/ kvacid bhāvanā samādhir iti pāṭhaḥ/ tatra bhāvanāsamādhī samūhasya
	saṃyamasyāvayavau hetū bhavataḥ/ vīryaṃ prayatnaḥ, tena maitryādibalavataḥ puṃsaḥ
	sukhitādiṣu pareṣāṃ kartavyeṣu prayatno+avandhyo bhavatīti/ upekṣaudāsīnyaṃ, na tatra
	bhāvanā nāpi sukhādivad bhāvyaṃ kiṃcid astīti //3.23//
children.translated_text: [Through <s>saṃyama</s>] on friendliness and the rest, strengths. From <s>saṃyama</s> on friendliness and the rest, he acquires the strengths of friendliness and the rest. Among these, from the cultivation of friendliness comes the strength by which one makes the world of living beings happy; thereby one becomes a benefactor of all. Similarly, from the strength of compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), one delivers living beings from suffering or from the cause of suffering. Similarly, from the strength of sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>), one establishes equanimity in the world of living beings. He states the causality of cultivation for <s>samādhi</s>, which is relevant to what will be discussed — 'the <s>samādhi</s> that comes from cultivation is the <s>saṃyama</s>.' Although <s>saṃyama</s> is indeed the triad of <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, and <s>samādhi</s> and not <s>samādhi</s> alone, nevertheless, since the effect arises immediately after <s>samādhi</s>, and due to the predominance of <s>samādhi</s>, <s>saṃyama</s> is figuratively attributed to it. In some readings: 'cultivation is <s>samādhi</s>.' In that case, cultivation and <s>samādhi</s> are the two components — the causes — of <s>saṃyama</s> as an aggregate. <s>Vīrya</s> (vigor) is effort; through that, the effort of a person possessing the strength of friendliness and the rest toward what is to be done for others who are happy, etc., becomes fruitful. Equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) is indifference; therein there is no cultivation, nor is there anything to be cultivated as in the case of happiness, etc. (3.23)

children.text: baleṣu hastibalādīni //3.24//
children.translated_text: [Through <s>saṃyama</s>] on strengths, [come] the strength of an elephant and the like. (3.24)

children.text: baleṣu hastibalādīni/ yasya bale saṃyamas tasya balaṃ labhata iti //3.24//
children.translated_text: [Through <s>saṃyama</s>] on strengths, the strength of an elephant and the like. One who performs <s>saṃyama</s> on strength obtains that strength. (3.24)

children.text: pravṛttyālokanyāsāt sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭajñānam //3.25//
children.translated_text: From directing the light of higher perception (<s>pravṛttyāloka</s>), knowledge of the subtle, concealed, and remote. (3.25)

children.text:
pravṛttyālokanyāsāt sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭajñānam/ sūkṣme vyavahite viprakṛṣṭe vārthe
	saṃyamena vinyasya tam adhigacchati //3.25//
children.translated_text: From directing the light of higher perception, knowledge of the subtle, concealed, and remote. Through <s>saṃyama</s> directed upon a subtle, concealed, or remote object, one attains knowledge of it. (3.25)

children.text: bhuvanajñānaṃ sūrye saṃyamāt //3.26//
children.translated_text: From <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun, knowledge of the worlds (<s>bhuvana</s>). (3.26)

children.text:
bhuvanajñānaṃ sūrye saṃyamāt/ ā dhruvādito merupṛṣṭhāt/ tad evam anena
	saṃgrahaślokāntena saṃkṣepataḥ sapta lokān upanyasya vistareṇāha --- tatrāvīcer iti/
	ghanaśabdena pṛthivy ucyate/ bhūmiḥ sthānam ity arthaḥ/ ete mahānarakā
	anekopanarakaparivārā boddhavyāḥ/ etān eva nāmāntareṇopasaṃharati --- maheti/ tasya
	sūryapracārād rātriṃdivaṃ lagnam iva vartate/

yam evāsya bhāgaṃ sūryas
	tyajati tatra rātriḥ/ yam eva bhāgam alaṃkaroti tatra dinam iti/
	sakalajambūdvīpaparimāṇam āha --- tad etad yojanaśatasāhasram/ kiṃbhūtaṃ yojanānāṃ
	śatasāhasram ity āha --- sumeror diśi diśi tadardhena pañcāśadyojanasahasreṇa vyūḍhaṃ
	saṃkṣiptam/ yato+asya madhyasthaḥ sumeruḥ samudrāś ca sarṣaparāśikalpā iti dviguṇā
	dviguṇā iti saṃbandhaḥ/ yathā sarṣaparāśir na vrīhirāśir ivocchrito nāpi bhūmisamas
	tathā samudrā apīty arthaḥ/ vicitraiḥ śailair avataṃsair iva saha vartanta iti
	savicitraśailāvataṃsā dvīpāḥ/ tad etat sarvaṃ sadvīpavipinanaganagaranīradhimālāvalayaṃ
	lokālokaparivṛtaṃ viśvaṃbharāmaṇḍalaṃ brahmāṇḍamadhye vyūḍhaṃ saṃkṣiptaṃ supratiṣṭhitaṃ
	saṃsthānaṃ saṃniveśo yasya tat tathoktam/ ye yatra prativasanti tatra tān darśayati ---
	tatra pātāla iti/ sumeroḥ saṃniveśam āha --- sumerur iti/ tad evaṃ bhūrlokaṃ saprakāram
	uktvā saprakāram evāntarīkṣalokam āha --- graheti/ vikṣepo vyāpāraḥ/
children.translated_text: abandons a region, there is night; where it adorns a region, there is day. He states the total measurement of <s>Jambudvīpa</s> (the Rose-apple continent) — 'that is one hundred thousand <s>yojanas</s>.' What kind of hundred thousand <s>yojanas</s>? He says — 'compacted, arranged in each direction from <s>Sumeru</s>, by half that, fifty thousand <s>yojanas</s>.' Because <s>Sumeru</s> stands in its center, and the oceans are like heaps of mustard seeds — the connection is 'doubled and doubled.' Just as a mustard heap is neither raised like a rice heap nor level with the ground, so too are the oceans — this is the meaning. 'Continents with picturesque mountain ornaments' — the continents exist together with varied mountains as though with ornaments. All this — the entire earth-disc with its continents, forests, trees, cities, and garlands of water-bodies, surrounded by <s>Lokāloka</s> (the boundary mountain) — is compacted, well-established within the cosmic egg (<s>brahmāṇḍa</s>); such is its arrangement and configuration, and thus it is described. He shows which beings reside where — 'therein, in the nether regions (<s>Pātāla</s>)' etc. He describes the arrangement of <s>Sumeru</s> — '<s>Sumeru</s>' etc. Having thus described the earthly world (<s>Bhūrloka</s>) with its details, he similarly describes the atmospheric world (<s>Antarīkṣa</s>) with its details — 'planets' etc. Movement (<s>vikṣepa</s>) means operation.

children.text:
svarlokam ādarśayati --- māhendranivāsina iti/ devanikāyā devajātayaḥ/ ṣaṇṇām api
	devanikāyānāṃ rūpotkarṣam āha --- sarve saṃkalpasiddhā iti/ saṃkalpamātrād evaiṣāṃ
	viṣayā upanamanti/ vṛndārakāḥ pūjyāḥ/ kāmabhogino maithunapriyāḥ/ aupapādikadehāḥ pitroḥ
	saṃyogam antareṇākasmād eva divyaṃ śarīram eṣāṃ dharmaviśeṣātisaṃskṛtebhyo+aṇubhyo
	bhūtebhyo bhavatīti/ maharlokam āha --- mahatīti/ mahābhūtavaśinaḥ/ yad yad etebhyo
	rocate tat tad eva mahābhūtāni prayacchanti/ tadicchātaś ca mahābhūtāni tena tena
	saṃsthānenāvatiṣṭhante/ dhyānāhārā dhyānamātratṛptāḥ pṛṣṭā bhavanti/ janalokam āha ---
	prathama ity uktakrameṇa/ bhūtendriyavaśina iti/ bhūtāni pṛthivyādīnīndriyāṇi śrotrādīni
	yathā niyoktum icchanti tathaiva niyujyante/ uktakramāpekṣayā dvitīyaṃ brahmaṇas
	tapolokam āha --- dvitīya iti/ bhūtendriyaprakṛtivaśina iti/ prakṛtiḥ pañca tanmātrāṇi
	tadvaśinas tadicchāto hi tanmātrāṇy eva kāyākāreṇa pariṇamanta ity āgaminaḥ/ dviguṇety
	ābhāsvarebhyo dviguṇāyuṣo mahābhāsvarās tebhyo 'pi dviguṇāyuṣaḥ satyamahābhāsvarā ity
	arthaḥ/ ūrdhvam ity ūrdhvaṃ satyaloke+apratihatajñānā avīces tu prabhṛty ā tapolokaṃ
	sūkṣmavyavahitādi sarvaṃ vijānantīty arthaḥ/ tṛtīyaṃ brahmaṇaḥ satyalokam āha ---
children.translated_text: He shows the celestial world (<s>Svarloka</s>) — 'the inhabitants of <s>Māhendra</s> [heaven]' etc. <s>Devanikāyas</s> are the classes of gods. He states the excellence of form for all six classes of gods — 'all [are] accomplished by mere intention' etc. The objects [of their desire] present themselves to them by mere intention alone. <s>Vṛndārakas</s> are the venerable ones. <s>Kāmabhogins</s> are those fond of sexual pleasures. They have 'spontaneously arisen bodies' (<s>aupapādika</s>) — without the union of parents, a divine body arises suddenly for them from atoms of the elements that are specially refined by their particular <s>dharma</s>. He describes <s>Maharloka</s> — 'the great' etc. [Its inhabitants are] masters of the great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>). Whatever pleases them, the great elements provide exactly that. And according to their wish, the great elements arrange themselves in whatever configuration. They are 'nourished by meditation' (<s>dhyānāhāra</s>) — satisfied by meditation alone, they become sated. He describes <s>Janaloka</s> — 'the first' etc., in the stated order. 'Masters of elements and senses' — they command the elements (earth, etc.) and the senses (hearing, etc.) to whatever function they wish, and those are so directed. With reference to the stated order, he describes <s>Tapoloka</s>, the second [world] of <s>Brahmā</s> — 'the second' etc. 'Masters of elements, senses, and their material cause (<s>prakṛti</s>)' — <s>prakṛti</s> here means the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements); they are masters of those, for according to their wish the <s>tanmātras</s> themselves transform into the form of the body — so say the traditionalists. 'Doubled' — from the <s>Ābhāsvaras</s>, the <s>Mahābhāsvaras</s> have double the lifespan, and from them the <s>Satyamahābhāsvaras</s> have double the lifespan — this is the meaning. 'Above' — above, in <s>Satyaloka</s>, [the inhabitants] have unobstructed knowledge; but from <s>Avīci</s> up to <s>Tapoloka</s>, they know everything subtle, concealed, and so forth — this is the meaning. He describes <s>Satyaloka</s>, the third [world] of <s>Brahmā</s> —

children.text:
tṛtīya iti/ akṛto bhavanasya gṛhasya nyāso yais te tathoktāḥ/ ādhārābhāvād
	eva svapratiṣṭhāḥ/ sveṣu śarīreṣu pratiṣṭhā yeṣāṃ te tathoktāḥ/ pradhānavaśinas
	tadicchātaḥ sattvarajastamāṃsi pravartante yāvatsargāyuṣaḥ/ tathā ca śrūyate ---
children.translated_text: The third [class of gods]. Those for whom no dwelling — no house — has been made, are so called. Due to the absence of a support, they are 'self-established' (<s>svapratiṣṭha</s>); those who are established in their own bodies are so called. Subject to <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial nature), by its will <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> operate for the duration of the creation-cycle. And thus it is heard [in scripture] —

From <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun, knowledge of the worlds. From <s>Dhruva</s> (the pole star) down to the summit of <s>Meru</s>. Having thus briefly presented the seven worlds in summary through a concluding verse, he expounds in detail — 'therein, from <s>Avīci</s>' etc. By the word 'solid' (<s>ghana</s>), earth is meant. 'Ground' (<s>bhūmi</s>) means location — this is the meaning. These great hells should be understood as accompanied by many subsidiary hells. He concludes these same [hells] under another name — '<s>mahā</s>' (great) etc. Due to the movement of the sun, day and night appear as though attached [to it]. Where the sun

children.text:
"brahmaṇā saha te sarve saṃprāpte pratisaṃcare/ parasyānte kṛtātmānaḥ praviśanti paraṃ
	padam"
kūrmapurāṇam pūrvakhaṇḍaḥ 12.269
children.translated_text: <s>Kūrmapurāṇa</s>, <s>Pūrvakhaṇḍa</s> 12.269

children.text: iti//
children.translated_text: Thus.
'Together with <s>Brahmā</s>, all of them, when dissolution arrives, being perfected selves, enter the supreme abode at the end of the higher [cycle].'

children.text:
tad evaṃ caturṇāṃ devanikāyānāṃ sādhāraṇadharmān uktvā nāmaviśeṣagrahaṇena
	dharmaviśeṣān āha --- tatreti/ acyutā nāma devāḥ sthūlaviṣayadhyānasukhās tena te
	tṛpyanti/ śuddhanivāsā nāma devāḥ sūkṣmaviṣayadhyānasukhās tena te tṛpyanti/ satyābhā
	nāma devā indriyaviṣayadhyānasukhās tena te tṛpyanti/ saṃjñāsaṃjñino nāma devā
	asmitāmātradhyānasukhās tena te tṛpyanti/ ta ete sarve saṃprajñātasamādhim upāsate/
	athāsaṃprajñātasamādhiniṣṭhā videhaprakṛtilayāḥ kasmān na lokamadhye nyasyanta ity ata
	āha --- videhaprakṛtilayās tv iti/ buddhivṛttimanto hi darśitaviṣayā lokayātrāṃ vahanto
	lokeṣu vartante/ na caivaṃ videhaprakṛtilayāḥ saty api sādhikāratva ity arthaḥ/ tad etad
	ā satyalokam ā cāvīcer yoginā sākṣātkaraṇīyaṃ, sūryadvāre suṣumnāyāṃ nāḍyām/ na
	caitāvatāpi tatsākṣātkāro bhavatīty ata āha --- evaṃ tāvad anyatrāpi suṣumnāyā anyatrāpi
	yogopādhyāyopadiṣṭeṣu yāvad idaṃ sarvaṃ jagad dṛṣṭam iti/ buddhisattvaṃ hi svabhāvata
	eva viśvaprakāśanasamarthaṃ tamomalāvṛtaṃ yatraiva rajasodghāṭyate tad eva prakāśayati/
	sūryadvārasaṃyamodghāṭitaṃ tu bhuvanaṃ prakāśayati/ na caivam anyatrāpi prasaṅgas
	tatsaṃyamasya tāvanmātrodghāṭanasāmarthyād iti sarvam avadātam //3.26//
children.translated_text: Having thus stated the common properties of the four classes of gods, he states the specific properties through the mention of specific names — 'Therein' etc. The gods called <s>Acyuta</s> have the bliss of meditation on gross objects; by that they are satisfied. The gods called <s>Śuddhanivāsa</s> have the bliss of meditation on subtle objects; by that they are satisfied. The gods called <s>Satyābha</s> have the bliss of meditation on sense-objects; by that they are satisfied. The gods called <s>Saṃjñāsaṃjñin</s> have the bliss of meditation on <s>asmitā</s> (egoity) alone; by that they are satisfied. All of these practice <s>saṃprajñāta samādhi</s> (cognitive absorption). Now, the <s>videhas</s> (disembodied) and <s>prakṛtilayas</s> (merged in <s>prakṛti</s>), who are established in <s>asaṃprajñāta samādhi</s> (non-cognitive absorption) — why are they not placed among the worlds? To this he says: 'But the <s>videhas</s> and <s>prakṛtilayas</s>' etc. For those possessing <s>buddhi</s>-modifications, having objects shown [to them], carrying on worldly activity, exist in the worlds. But not so the <s>videhas</s> and <s>prakṛtilayas</s>, even though they possess a residual basis — this is the meaning. This entire [realm] from <s>Satyaloka</s> to <s>Avīci</s> is to be directly realized by the <s>yogin</s>, at the solar gateway, in the <s>suṣumnā</s> <s>nāḍī</s> (channel). But even with this much, direct realization of that does not occur — to this he says: 'Thus, even elsewhere, beyond the <s>suṣumnā</s>, and in [whatever] the <s>yoga</s> teacher instructs, until this entire universe has been seen.' For <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, by its very nature capable of illuminating the universe, covered by the impurity of <s>tamas</s>, illuminates only that [region] where it is opened up by <s>rajas</s>. When opened by <s>saṃyama</s> at the solar gateway, it illuminates the [cosmic] realm. Nor does this [reasoning] extend to other [cases], because that <s>saṃyama</s> has the capacity to open up only that much — thus everything is clear. (3.26)

children.text: candre tārāvyūhajñānam //3.27//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the moon, knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. (3.27)

children.text: dhruve tadgatijñānam //3.28//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the pole star, knowledge of their movements. (3.28)

children.text: nābhicakre kāyavyūhajñānam //3.29//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the navel circle (<s>nābhicakra</s>), knowledge of the arrangement of the body. (3.29)

children.text: kaṇṭhakūpe kṣutpipāsānivṛttiḥ //3.30//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the throat well (<s>kaṇṭhakūpa</s>), cessation of hunger and thirst. (3.30)

children.text: kūrmanāḍyāṃ sthairyam //3.31//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the <s>kūrma-nāḍī</s> (tortoise channel), steadiness. (3.31)

children.text:
candre tārāvyūhajñānam/ dhruve tadgatijñānam/ nābhicakre kāyavyūhajñānam/ kaṇṭhakūpe
	kṣutpipāsānivṛttiḥ/ kūrmanāḍyāṃ sthairyam/ tatra tatra jijñāsāyāṃ yoginas tatra tatra
	saṃyamaḥ/ evaṃ kṣutpipāsānivṛttihetuḥ saṃyamaḥ sthairyahetuś ca sūtrapadair upadiṣṭo
	bhāṣyeṇa ca nigadavyākhyātena vyākhyāta iti na vyākhyātaḥ //3.27//3.28//3.29//3.30//3.31//
children.translated_text: '[From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the moon, knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the pole star, knowledge of their movements. [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the navel circle, knowledge of the arrangement of the body. [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the throat well, cessation of hunger and thirst. [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the <s>kūrma-nāḍī</s>, steadiness.' In each case, when there is a desire to know about that [subject], the <s>yogin</s> performs <s>saṃyama</s> on that [object]. Thus the <s>saṃyama</s> that is the cause of the cessation of hunger and thirst, and the cause of steadiness, has been taught by the <s>sūtra</s> words and explained by the <s>bhāṣya</s> through direct statement (<s>nigada</s>)-explanation — hence [I have] not commented [further]. (3.27)(3.28)(3.29)(3.30)(3.31)

children.text: mūrdhajyotiṣi siddhadarśanam //3.32//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the light at the crown of the head, the vision of <s>siddhas</s> (perfected beings). (3.32)

children.text: mūrdhajyotiṣi siddhadarśanam/ mūrdhaśabdena suṣumnā nāḍī lakṣyate tatra saṃyama iti //3.32//
children.translated_text: '[From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the light at the crown of the head, the vision of <s>siddhas</s>.' By the word 'crown' (<s>mūrdhan</s>), the <s>suṣumnā nāḍī</s> is indicated; <s>saṃyama</s> is [performed] there. (3.32)

children.text: prātibhād vā sarvam //3.33//
children.translated_text: Or, from <s>prātibha</s> (intuitive illumination), everything [is known]. (3.33)

children.text:
prātibhād vā sarvam/ pratibhohas tadbhavaṃ prātibham/ prasaṃkhyānahetusaṃyamavato hi
	tatprakarṣe prasaṃkhyānodayapūrvaliṅgaṃ yad ūhajaṃ jñānaṃ tena sarvaṃ vijānāti yogī/ tac
	ca prasaṃkhyānasaṃnidhāpanena saṃsārāt tārayatīti tārakam //3.33//
children.translated_text: 'Or, from <s>prātibha</s>, everything.' <s>Prātibha</s> means that which arises from <s>pratibhā</s> (intuitive flash). For one who possesses the <s>saṃyama</s> that is the cause of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (discernment), at the culmination of that [practice], the knowledge born of <s>ūha</s> (reasoning), which is the precursory sign of the arising of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> — by that the <s>yogin</s> knows everything. And that [knowledge], by bringing about the proximity of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, delivers [the <s>yogin</s>] from <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) — hence it is called <s>tāraka</s> (liberating). (3.33)

children.text: hṛdaye cittasaṃvit //3.34//
children.translated_text: [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the heart, understanding of <s>citta</s> (mind). (3.34)

children.text:
hṛdaye cittasaṃvit/ hṛdayapadaṃ vyācaṣṭe --- yad idam asmin brahmapure/ bṛhattvād ātmā
	brahma tasya puraṃ nilayas tad dhi tatra vijānāti svam iti/ daharaṃ gartaṃ tad eva
	puṇḍarīkam adhomukhaṃ veśma manasaḥ/ cittasaṃvedanatve hetum āha --- tatra vijñānaṃ
	tatra saṃyamāc cittaṃ vijānāti svavṛttiviśiṣṭam //3.34//
children.translated_text: '[From <s>saṃyama</s>] on the heart, understanding of <s>citta</s>.' He explains the word 'heart' — 'That which is in this city of <s>Brahman</s>.' Due to its greatness, the Self is <s>Brahman</s>; its city is its abode; for it knows itself there. The small cavity — that very lotus-[space], facing downward — is the dwelling of the mind. He states the reason for the understanding of <s>citta</s> — 'There is consciousness' — through <s>saṃyama</s> there, one knows <s>citta</s> as qualified by its own modifications. (3.34)

children.text:
sattvapuruṣayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ parārthāt svārthasaṃyamāt
	  puruṣajñānam //3.35//
children.translated_text: Since <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> are absolutely unmixed, the non-distinction of cognition is <s>bhoga</s> (experience); from <s>saṃyama</s> on one's own purpose, distinct from [<s>sattva</s>'s] purpose for another, [arises] the knowledge of <s>puruṣa</s>. (3.35)

children.text:
sattvapuruṣayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayoḥ pratyayāviśeṣo bhogaḥ parārthāt svārthasaṃyamāt
	puruṣajñānam/ yatra prakāśarūpasyātisvacchasya nitāntābhibhūtarajastamastayā
	vivekakhyātirūpeṇa pariṇatasya buddhisattvasyātyantikaś caitanyād asaṃkaras tatra kaiva
	kathā rajastamasor jaḍasvabhāvayor ity āśayavān sūtrakāraḥ sattvapuruṣayor ity uvāca/
	imam evābhiprāyaṃ gṛhītvā bhāṣyakāro 'py āha --- buddhisattvaṃ prakhyāśīlam iti/ na
	prakhyāśīlamātram api tu vivekakhyātirūpeṇa pariṇatam ato
	nitāntaśuddhaprakāśatayātyantasārūpyaṃ caitanyeneti saṃkara ity ata āha --- samāneti/
	sattvenopanibandhanam avinābhāvaḥ saṃbandhaḥ, samānaṃ sattvopanibandhanaṃ yayo
	rajastamasos te tathokte/ vaśīkāro+abhibhavaḥ/ asaṃkaram āha ---

tasmāc
	ceti/ cakāro+apyarthaḥ/ na kevalaṃ rajastamobhyām ity arthaḥ/ pariṇāmina iti vaidharmyam
	apariṇāminaḥ puruṣād uktam/ pratyayāviśeṣaḥ śāntaghoramūḍharūpāyā buddheś
	caitanyabimbodgrāheṇa caitanyasya śāntādyākārādhyāropaś candramasa iva
	svacchasalilapratibimbitasya tatkampāt kampanāropaḥ/ bhogahetum āha ---
	darśitaviṣayatvād iti/ asakṛd vyākhyātam/ nanu buddhisattvam astu puruṣabhinnaṃ bhogas
	tu puṃsaḥ kuto bhidyata ity ata āha --- sa bhogapratyayo bhogarūpaḥ pratyayaḥ
	sattvasyātaḥ parārthatvād dṛśyo bhogyaḥ/ sattvaṃ hi parārthaṃ saṃhatatvāt taddharmaś ca
	bhoga iti so 'pi parārthaḥ/ yasmai ca parasmā asau tasya bhoktur bhogyaḥ/
	athavānukūlapratikūlavedanīyas tu sukhaduḥkhānubhavo bhogaḥ/ na cāyam ātmānam
	evānukūlayati pratikūlayati vā, svātmani vṛttivirodhād ato+anukūlanīyapratikūlanīyārtho
	bhogaḥ/ sa bhoktātmā tasya dṛśyo bhogya iti/ yas tu tasmāt parārthād viśiṣṭa iti/
	parārthād iti pañcamyanyapadādhyāhāreṇa vyākhyātā/ syād etat puruṣaviṣayā cet prajñā
	hanta bhoḥ puruṣaḥ prajñāyāḥ prajñeya iti prajñāntaram eva tatra tatrety anavasthāpāta
	ity ata āha --- na ca puruṣapratyayeneti/ ayam abhisaṃdhiḥ --- cityā jaḍaḥ prakāśyate/
	na jaḍena citiḥ/ puruṣapratyayas tv acidātmā kathaṃ cidātmānaṃ prakāśayet/ cidātmā tv
	aparādhīnaprakāśo jaḍaṃ prakāśayatīti yuktam/ buddhisattvātmanety acidrūpatādātmyena
	jaḍatvam āha/ buddhisattvagatapuruṣapratibimbālambanāt puruṣālambanaṃ na tu
	puruṣaprakāśanāt puruṣālambanam/ buddhisattvam eva tu tena pratyayena
	saṃkrāntapuruṣapratibimbaṃ puruṣacchāyāpannaṃ caitanyam ālambata iti puruṣārthaḥ/
	atraiva śrutim udāharati --- tathā hy uktam īśvareṇa vijñātāram iti/ na kenacid ity
	arthaḥ //3.35//
children.translated_text: 'Therefore, also' etc. The particle 'ca' has the sense of 'api' (even). The meaning is: not only from <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. 'Being subject to transformation' states the difference from <s>puruṣa</s> who does not transform. The 'non-distinction of cognition' is the superimposition upon consciousness of the tranquil, fierce, and deluded forms of <s>buddhi</s> through [<s>buddhi</s>'s] capacity to receive the reflection of consciousness — like the superimposition of trembling upon the moon when reflected in clear water due to the trembling of that [water]. He states the cause of <s>bhoga</s> (experience) — 'Because objects have been shown' etc. This has been explained repeatedly. But even if <s>buddhi-sattva</s> is different from <s>puruṣa</s>, why should <s>bhoga</s> belong to <s>puruṣa</s>? To this he says: 'That cognition of experience, the cognition having the form of experience, belongs to <s>sattva</s>; hence, because of being for another's purpose, it is visible, enjoyable.' For <s>sattva</s> is for another's purpose since it is composite; and <s>bhoga</s>, being its property, is also for another's purpose. And the one for whom, the other, [<s>bhoga</s>] belongs — it is enjoyable for that experiencer. Or alternatively, the experience of pleasure and pain, to be felt as favorable or unfavorable, is <s>bhoga</s>. And this [<s>bhoga</s>] does not make itself favorable or unfavorable, since there would be a contradiction of activity directed at oneself; therefore <s>bhoga</s> requires one to be made favorable or unfavorable to. That experiencer-Self — for him it is visible, enjoyable. 'But that which is distinct from the purpose for another' — 'from the purpose for another' is explained by supplying the word 'different' with the ablative. One might object: if the cognition concerns <s>puruṣa</s>, then <s>puruṣa</s> is the knowable of that cognition, and so another cognition [is needed to know] that, and so on — leading to infinite regress — to this he says: 'Not by a cognition of <s>puruṣa</s>' etc. The intention is this: consciousness illuminates the inert; the inert does not [illuminate] consciousness. But the cognition of <s>puruṣa</s> is non-conscious in nature — how could it illuminate what is conscious in nature? But the conscious, whose illumination is not dependent on another, illuminates the inert — this is fitting. 'Having the nature of <s>buddhi-sattva</s>' — he states the inertness through its identity with the non-conscious nature. The cognition has <s>puruṣa</s> as its object because it is based on the reflection of <s>puruṣa</s> in <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, not because it illuminates <s>puruṣa</s> [directly]. Rather, <s>buddhi-sattva</s> itself, into which the reflection of <s>puruṣa</s> has passed through that cognition, having assumed the semblance of consciousness, takes consciousness as its object — hence [<s>saṃyama</s>] is for the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s>. Here he cites a <s>śruti</s> (scriptural passage) — 'As has been said by the Lord: the knower' etc. 'By no one' — this is the meaning. (3.35)

'Since <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> are absolutely unmixed, the non-distinction of cognition is experience; from <s>saṃyama</s> on one's own purpose, distinct from the purpose for another, the knowledge of <s>puruṣa</s>.' Where <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, whose nature is illumination, being supremely transparent, having utterly subdued <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, having transformed into the form of <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment) — [there] its absolute non-mixture with consciousness [is manifest]; then what need even to speak of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, whose nature is inert? With this intention the author of the <s>sūtras</s> said '<s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>.' Grasping this very intention, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) also says: '<s>buddhi-sattva</s> has the nature of illumination' etc. Not merely having the nature of illumination, but having transformed into the form of <s>vivekakhyāti</s>; therefore, through its supremely pure luminosity, there is extreme similarity with consciousness — hence the confusion — to this he says: 'Equal' etc. The connection (<s>upanibandha</s>) with <s>sattva</s> means the inseparable relation; those whose connection with <s>sattva</s> is equal — namely <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> — are so called. '<s>Vaśīkāra</s>' means subjugation. He states the non-mixture —

children.text: tataḥ prātibhaśrāvaṇavedanādarśāsvādavārtā jāyante //3.36//
children.translated_text: From that arise <s>prātibha</s> (intuitive), <s>śrāvaṇa</s> (auditory), <s>vedanā</s> (tactile), <s>ādarśa</s> (visual), <s>āsvāda</s> (gustatory), and <s>vārtā</s> (olfactory) [cognitions]. (3.36)

children.text:
sa ca svārthasaṃyamo na yāvat pradhānaṃ svakāryaṃ puruṣajñānam abhinirvartayati tāvat
	tasya purastād yā vibhūtīr ādhatte tāḥ sarvā darśayati --- tataḥ
	prātibhaśrāvaṇavedanādarśāsvādavārtā jāyante/ tad anena yogajadharmānugṛhītānāṃ
	manaḥśrotratvakcakṣurjihvāghrāṇānāṃ yathāsaṃkhyaṃ
	prātibhajñānadivyaśabdādyaparokṣahetubhāvā uktāḥ/ śrotrādīnāṃ pañcānāṃ
	divyaśabdādyupalambhakānāṃ tāntrikyaḥ saṃjñāḥ śrāvaṇādyāḥ/ sugamaṃ bhāṣyam //3.36//
children.translated_text: And that <s>saṃyama</s> on one's own purpose — before it produces its principal effect, namely the knowledge of <s>puruṣa</s> — he shows all the supernatural powers it bestows prior to that — 'From that arise <s>prātibha</s>, <s>śrāvaṇa</s>, <s>vedanā</s>, <s>ādarśa</s>, <s>āsvāda</s>, and <s>vārtā</s> [cognitions].' By this, the causal roles of the mind, ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose — respectively favored by <s>yoga</s>-born properties — for <s>prātibha</s> knowledge, divine sound, and the other direct perceptions, have been stated in corresponding order. The <s>tāntrika</s> (technical) designations of the five [senses] — ear and the rest — which apprehend divine sound and the like, are <s>śrāvaṇa</s> and the others. The <s>bhāṣya</s> is easy to understand. (3.36)

children.text: te samādhāv upasargā vyutthāne siddhayaḥ //3.37//
children.translated_text: These are obstacles to <s>samādhi</s> (absorption), but powers in the state of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>). (3.37)

children.text:
kadācid ātmaviṣayasaṃyame pravṛttas tatprabhāvād amūr arthāntarasiddhīr adhigamya
	kṛtārthamanyaḥ saṃyamād viramed ata āha --- te samādhāv upasargā vyutthāne siddhayaḥ/
	vyutthitacitto hi tāḥ siddhīr abhimanyate/ janmadurgata iva draviṇakaṇikām api
	draviṇasaṃbhāram/ yoginā tu samāhitacittenopanatābhyo+api tābhyo virantavyam/
	abhisaṃhitatāpatrayātyantikopaśamarūpaparamapuruṣārthaḥ sa khalv ayaṃ kathaṃ
	tatpratyanīkāsu siddhiṣu rajyeteti sūtrabhāṣyayor arthaḥ //3.37//
children.translated_text: Lest [the yogin], while engaged in <s>saṃyama</s> directed toward the Self, might attain these incidental supernatural powers (<s>siddhis</s>) through the influence of that [saṃyama], and considering himself fulfilled, might desist from <s>saṃyama</s> — hence he says: 'These are obstacles to <s>samādhi</s>, though they are powers in the state of outward-directed [mind].' For one whose mind is outward-directed regards those powers highly — like one born in poverty [who regards] even a small bit of wealth as a great fortune. But the <s>yogin</s> with concentrated mind should turn away even from those [powers] when they present themselves. For one who has set his aim on the supreme human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), which is the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering — how could he be attached to <s>siddhis</s> that are opposed to that? Such is the meaning of both the <s>sūtra</s> and the <s>bhāṣya</s>. (3.37)

children.text: bandhakāraṇaśaithilyāt pracārasaṃvedanāc ca cittasya paraśarīrāveśaḥ //3.38//
children.translated_text: From the loosening of the cause of bondage and from the knowledge of the pathways of the mind, [there arises] the entering of another's body. (3.38)

children.text:
tad evaṃ jñānarūpam aiśvaryaṃ puruṣadarśanāntaṃ saṃyamaphalam uktvā kriyārūpam
	aiśvaryaṃ saṃyamaphalam āha --- bandhakāraṇaśaithilyāt pracārasaṃvedanāc ca cittasya
	paraśarīrāveśaḥ/

samādhibalād iti/ bandhakāraṇaviṣayasaṃyamabalāt
	prādhānyāt samādhigrahaṇam/ pracaraty anenāsminn iti pracāraḥ/ cittasya gamāgamādhvāno
	nāḍyas tasmin pracāre saṃyamāt tadvedanaṃ, tasmāc ca bandhakāraṇaśaithilyān na tena
	pratibadhyate/ apratibaddham apy unmārgeṇa gacchan na svaśarīrād apratyūhaṃ niṣkrāmati/
	na ca paraśarīram āviśati/ tasmāt tatpracāro+api jñātavyaḥ/ indriyāṇi ca cittānusārīṇi
	paraśarīre yathādhiṣṭhānaṃ niviśanta iti //3.38//
children.translated_text: 'By the power of <s>samādhi</s>' — because the power of <s>saṃyama</s> directed toward the cause of bondage is predominant, '<s>samādhi</s>' is mentioned [as representative]. '<s>Pracāra</s>' (pathway) — that by which and in which [the mind] moves. The <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels) are the pathways of the mind's coming and going; from <s>saṃyama</s> on that pathway [comes] the knowledge of it; and from the loosening of the cause of bondage, [the mind] is not obstructed by that [bondage]. Yet even when unobstructed, if going by a wrong path, it does not exit from one's own body without hindrance, nor does it enter another's body. Therefore, the pathway too must be known. And the sense organs, following the mind, enter the other body according to its [new] abode. (3.38)

Thus, having stated the sovereignty that takes the form of knowledge and culminates in the vision of <s>Puruṣa</s> as the fruit of <s>saṃyama</s>, he states the sovereignty that takes the form of action as the fruit of <s>saṃyama</s> — 'From the loosening of the cause of bondage and from the knowledge of the pathways of the mind, the entering of another's body.'

children.text: udānajayāj jalapaṅkakaṇṭakādiṣv asaṅga utkrāntiś ca //3.39//
children.translated_text: From mastery of <s>udāna</s> (the upward-moving vital breath), [there arises] non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and [the power of] ascent [at death]. (3.39)

children.text:
udānajayāj jalapaṅkakaṇṭakādiṣv asaṅga utkrāntiś ca/ samastendriyavṛttir jīvanaṃ
	prāṇādilakṣaṇā prāṇādayo lakṣaṇaṃ yasyāḥ sā tathoktā/ dvayīndriyāṇāṃ vṛttir
	bāhyābhyantarī ca/ bāhyā rūpādyālocanalakṣaṇā/ ābhyantarī tu jīvanaṃ, sā hi
	prayatnabhedaḥ śarīropagṛhītamārutakriyābhedahetuḥ sarvakaraṇasādhāraṇaḥ/ yathāhuḥ
	---
children.translated_text: From mastery of <s>udāna</s>, non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and ascent. The activity of all the senses collectively is life — [which is] characterized by <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and the rest. The activity of the senses is twofold: external and internal. The external [activity] is characterized by the apprehension of form and the like. But the internal [activity] is life itself; for that is the differentiation of effort which is the cause of the differentiation of the activities of the air (<s>vāyu</s>) held within the body, and is common to all instruments [of cognition]. As they say —

children.text: "sāmānyakaraṇavṛttiḥ prāṇādyā vāyavaḥ pañca"
sāṃkhyakārikā 29
children.translated_text: [Reference: <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 29]

children.text: iti/
children.translated_text: Thus.
'The general function of the instruments [of cognition] is the fivefold vital breaths such as <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest.'

children.text:
tair asya lakṣaṇīyatvāt tasya prayatnasya kriyā kāryaṃ pañcatayī/ prāṇa ā nāsikāgrād ā
	ca hṛdayād avasthitaḥ/ aśitapītāhārapariṇatibhedaṃ rasaṃ tatra tatra sthāne samam
	anurūpaṃ nayan samānaḥ/ ā hṛdayād ā ca nābher asyāvasthānam/ mūtrapurīṣagarbhādīnām
	apanayanahetur apānaḥ/ ā

nābher ā ca pādatalād asya vṛttiḥ/ unnayanād
	ūrdhvaṃ nayanād rasādīnām udānaḥ/ ā nāsikāgrād ā ca śiraso vṛttir asya/ vyāpī vyānaḥ/
	eṣām uktānāṃ pradhānaṃ prāṇas tadutkrame sarvotkramaśruteḥ "prāṇam utkrāmantam anu sarve
	prāṇā utkrāmanti"
children.translated_text: its [<s>apāna</s>'s] function extends from the navel to the soles of the feet. <s>Udāna</s>, so called from carrying upward (<s>unnayana</s>) the <s>rasa</s> and the like — its function extends from the tip of the nose to the top of the head. <s>Vyāna</s> is the all-pervading one. Among those mentioned, <s>prāṇa</s> is the chief, since upon its departure all others depart, as stated in scripture: '<s>prāṇa</s>'

children.text: bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣat 4.4.2
children.translated_text: [Reference: <s>Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad</s> 4.4.2]

children.text:
iti/ tad evaṃ prāṇādīnāṃ
	kriyāsthānabhedena bhedaṃ pratipādya sūtrārtham avatārayati --- udānajayād iti/ udāne
	kṛtasaṃyamas tajjayāj jalādibhir na pratihanyate/ utkrāntiś cārcirādimārgeṇa bhavati
	prāyaṇakāle/ tasmāt tām utkrāntiṃ vaśitvena pratipadyate/ prāṇādisaṃyamāt tadvijaye
	bhūtajaya etāḥ kriyāḥ sthānavijayādibhedāt pratipattavyāḥ //3.39//
