children.translated_text: The past and future exist in their own nature, due to the difference in the paths (<s>adhvan</s>) of the <s>dharmas</s>. //4.12//

children.text:
uttarasūtram avatārayituṃ śaṅkate --- nāstīti/ asata iti tu saṃpātāyātaṃ nidarśanāya
      vā/ atītānāgataṃ svarūpato 'sty adhvabhedād dharmāṇām/ nāsatām utpādo na satāṃ vināśaḥ
      kiṃ tu satām eva dharmāṇām adhvabhedapariṇāma evodayavyayāv iti sūtrārthaḥ/ anubhūtā
      prāptā yena vyaktis tat tathā/ saṃprati vyaktir nāstīti yāvat/ itaś ca traikālye 'pi
      dharmaḥ sann ity āha --- yadi ceti/ na hy asañjñānaviṣayaḥ saṃbhavatīti nirupākhyatvād
      viṣayāvabhāsaṃ hi vijñānaṃ nāsati viṣaye bhavati/ traikālyaviṣayaṃ ca vijñānaṃ yoginām
      asmadādīnāṃ ca vijñānam asati viṣaye notpannaṃ syāt/ utpadyate ca/ tasmād atītānāgate
      sāmānyarūpeṇa samanugate sta iti/ evam anubhavato jñānaṃ viṣayasattve hetur uktam/
      uddeśyatvād apy anāgatasya viṣayatvena sattvam evety āha --- kiṃ ca bhogabhāgīyasyeti/
      kuśalo nipuṇaḥ/ anuṣṭheye+api ca yad yan nimittaṃ tat sarvaṃ naimittike saty eva viśeṣam
      ādhatte/ yathā kāṇḍalāvavedādhyāyādayaḥ/ na khalv ete kāṇḍalāvādayo 'santam utpādayanti/
      sata eva tu tatprāptivikārau kurvanti/ evaṃ kulālādayo+api sata eva ghaṭasya
      vartamānībhāvahetava ity āha --- sataś ceti/ yadi tu vartamānatvābhāvād atītānāgatayor
      asattvaṃ hanta bho vartamānasyāpy abhāvo+atītānāgatatvābhāvāt/ adhvaviśiṣṭatayā tu
      sattvaṃ trayāṇām apy aviśiṣṭam ity abhiprāyeṇāha

--- dharmī ceti/
      pratyekam avasthānaṃ pratyavasthitir iti/ dravyata iti dravye dharmiṇi sārvavibhaktikas
      tasiḥ/ yady atītānāgatāv atītānāgatatve na stas tarhi vartamānasamaye tattvābhāvān na
      syātām ity ata āha --- ekasya ceti/ prakṛtam upasaṃharati --- iti nābhūtvā bhāva iti //4.12//
children.translated_text: 'And the <s>dharmin</s> (property-bearer)' and so on. Individual standing is establishment in each [time]. 'In terms of substance' — the <s>tasi</s> suffix is used in all case-senses with respect to substance, i.e., the <s>dharmin</s>. If the past and future do not possess pastness and futurity, then due to the absence of their reality at the present time, they would not exist — to this he says: 'And of the one' and so on. He concludes the topic under discussion — 'Thus, there is no coming into being from non-being.' //4.12//

To introduce the next <s>sūtra</s>, he raises a doubt — 'It does not exist' and so on. 'Of the non-existent' is used for emphasis or as an illustration. The past and future exist in their own nature, due to the difference in the paths of the <s>dharmas</s>. There is no arising of the non-existent, nor destruction of the existent; rather, for existent <s>dharmas</s> alone, the transformation of paths is itself the arising and passing away — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>. 'Experienced' means that by which manifestation has been attained; 'at present, manifestation does not exist' — this much is meant. And for this further reason, <s>dharma</s> exists even in all three times, he says — 'And if' and so on. For an object of non-consciousness is not possible — because of being without designation — knowledge is a reflection of the object and does not arise in the absence of an object. And the knowledge of <s>yogins</s>, and the knowledge of us ordinary people, pertaining to all three times, would not arise if the object did not exist.

children.text: te vyaktasūkṣmā guṇātmānaḥ //4.13//
children.translated_text: They are manifest or subtle, of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>. //4.13//

children.text:
syād etat/ ayaṃ tu nānāprakāro dharmidharmāvasthāpariṇāmarūpo viśvabhedaprapañco na
      pradhānād ekasmād bhavitum arhati/ na hy avilakṣaṇāt kāraṇāt kāryabhedasaṃbhava ity ata
      āha --- te vyaktasūkṣmā guṇātmānaḥ/ te tryadhvāno dharmā vyaktāś ca sūkṣmāś ca guṇātmāno
      na traiguṇyātiriktam eṣām asti kāraṇam/ vaicitryaṃ tu tadāhitānādikleśavāsanānugatād
      vaicitryāt/ yathoktaṃ vāyupurāṇe ---
children.translated_text: There might be this [objection]: But this diverse elaboration of the world, consisting of the transformation of <s>dharmin</s>, <s>dharma</s>, and <s>avasthā</s> (condition), of manifold differences, cannot arise from a single <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter). For from a cause that is undifferentiated, a differentiation of effects is not possible — to this he says: 'They are manifest or subtle, of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>.' Those <s>dharmas</s> of the three time-paths are manifest and subtle, of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> — there is no cause for them beyond the three <s>guṇas</s>. Their diversity, however, comes from the diversity of the beginningless <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>vāsanās</s> (impressions) deposited by them. As stated in the <s>Vāyupurāṇa</s> —

children.text: "vaiśvarūpyāt pradhānasya pariṇāmo+ayam adbhutaḥ"
vāyupurāṇam 53.120
children.translated_text: <s>Vāyupurāṇa</s> 53.120

children.text: iti/
children.translated_text: Thus.
"From the multiformity of <s>Pradhāna</s>, this transformation is wondrous."

children.text:
vyaktānāṃ pṛthivyādīnām ekādaśendriyāṇāṃ ca vartamānānām atītānāgatatvaṃ ṣaḍaviśeṣā
      yathāyogaṃ bhavanti/ saṃprati viśvasya nityānityarūpe vibhajan nityarūpam āha --- sarvam
      idam iti/ dṛśyamānaṃ saṃniveśaḥ saṃsthānabhedavān pariṇāma ity arthaḥ/ atraiva
      ṣaṣṭitantraśāstrasyānuśiṣṭiḥ/

māyeva na tu māyā/ sutucchakaṃ vināśi/ yathā
      hi māyāhnāyaivānyathā bhavati evaṃ vikārā apy āvirbhāvatirobhāvadharmāṇaḥ pratikṣaṇam
      anyathā/ prakṛtir nityatayā māyāvidharmiṇī paramārtheti //4.13//
children.translated_text: Like <s>māyā</s> (illusion) but not <s>māyā</s>. Extremely insubstantial and perishable. For just as <s>māyā</s> becomes different by the very course of <s>māyā</s>, so too the <s>vikāras</s> (modifications), whose nature is appearance and disappearance, become different every moment. <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), being eternal, is unlike <s>māyā</s> and is the ultimate reality. //4.13//

The manifest [entities] — earth and the other [elements], and the eleven sense organs — when in the present, their becoming past or future constitutes the six <s>aviśeṣas</s> (non-specifics), as applicable. Now, distinguishing the eternal and non-eternal aspects of the universe, he states the eternal aspect — 'All this' and so on. 'Visible' [means] configuration — transformation possessing differences of form — this is the meaning. Here itself is the teaching of the <s>Ṣaṣṭitantra</s> (Sixty-Topic Treatise).

children.text: pariṇāmaikatvād vastutattvam //4.14//
children.translated_text: Due to the oneness of transformation, [there is] the reality of the object. //4.14//

children.text:
bhavatu traiguṇyasyetthaṃ pariṇāmavaicitryam ekas tu pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīti vā toyam iti
      vā kuta ātmana ekatvavirodhād ity āśaṅkya sūtram avatārayati --- yadā tu sarve guṇā iti/
      pariṇāmaikatvād vastutattvam/ bahūnām apy ekaḥ pariṇāmo dṛṣṭaḥ/ tadyathā
      gavāśvamahiṣamātaṅgānāṃ rumānikṣiptānām eko lavaṇatvajātīyalakṣaṇaḥ pariṇāmo
      vartitailānalānāṃ ca pradīpa iti/ evaṃ bahutve+api guṇānāṃ pariṇāmaikatvaṃ, tatas
      tanmātrabhūtabhautikānāṃ pratyekaṃ tattvam ekatvam/ grahaṇātmakānāṃ sattvapradhānatayā
      prakāśātmanām ahaṃkārāvāntarakāryāṇāṃ karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotram indriyam/
      teṣām eva guṇānāṃ tamaḥpradhānatayā jaḍatvena grāhyātmakānāṃ śabdatanmātrabhāvenaikaḥ
      pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣayaḥ/ śabda iti śabdatanmātram/ viṣaya iti jaḍatvam āha na tu
      tanmātrasya śrotraviṣayatvasaṃbhava iti/ śeṣaṃ sugamam/ atha vijñānavādinaṃ vaināśikam
      utthāpayati --- nāsty artho vijñānavisahacara iti/ yadi hi bhūtabhautikāni vijñānamātrād
      bhinnāni bhaveyus tatas tadutpattikāraṇam īdṛśaṃ pradhānaṃ kalpyeta, na tu tāni
      vijñānātiriktāni santi paramārthataḥ/ tat kathaṃ pradhānakalpanaṃ kathaṃ ca grahaṇānām
      indriyāṇām ahaṃkāravikārāṇāṃ kalpaneti/ tathā hi --- jaḍasyārthasya svayam aprakāśatvān
      nāsty artho vijñānavisahacaraḥ/ sāhacaryaṃ saṃbandhaḥ/ tadabhāvo visahacaratvam/

vir abhāvārthaḥ/ vijñānāsaṃbandho nāsti vyavahārayogya ity arthaḥ/ asti tu
      jñānam arthavisahacaraṃ tasya svayaṃprakāśatvena svagocarāstitāvyavahāre kartavye jaḍam
      arthaṃ pratyapekṣābhāvāt/ tad anena vedyatvasahopalambhaniyamau sūcitau vijñānavādinā/
      tau caivaṃ prayogam ārohataḥ --- yad vedyate yena vedanena tat tato na bhidyate/ yathā
      jñānasyātmā/ vedyante ca bhūtabhautikānīti viruddhavyāptopalabdhir
      niṣedhyabhedaviruddhenābhedena vyāptaṃ vedyatvaṃ dṛśyamānaṃ svavyāpakam abhedam
      upasthāpayat tadviruddhaṃ bhedaṃ pratikṣipatīti/ tathā yad yena niyatasahopalambhaṃ tat
      tato na bhidyate/ yathaikasmāc candrād dvitīyaś candraḥ/ niyatasahopalambhaś cārtho
      jñāneneti vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhiḥ/ niṣedhyabhedavyāpakāniyamaviruddho niyamo+aniyamaṃ
      nivartayaṃs tadvyāptaṃ bhedaṃ pratikṣipatīti/ syād etat/ arthaś cen na bhinno jñānāt
      kathaṃ bhinnavat pratibhāsata ity ata āha --- kalpitam iti/ yathāhur vaināśikāḥ ---
children.translated_text: '<s>Vi</s>' has the sense of absence. '[An object] unrelated to cognition does not exist' — meaning it has no capacity for practical activity. But cognition does exist as unassociated with objects, since being self-luminous, in carrying out the practical activity of affirming the existence of its own object, it has no dependence on an inert object. By this, the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> has indicated [two arguments]: the rule of cognizability (<s>vedyatva</s>) and the rule of co-perception (<s>sahopalambhaniyama</s>). These amount to the following formal arguments: whatever is cognized by a certain cognition is not different from it — like the self of cognition itself. And the elements and their products are cognized — this is an 'apprehension of a property pervaded by the contradictory of the [property] to be negated': cognizability, being seen to be pervaded by non-difference (which contradicts the difference to be negated), by bringing to mind its pervader — non-difference — thereby refutes difference, which contradicts it. Similarly: whatever is invariably co-perceived with something is not different from it — like the second moon [which is not different] from the one moon. And the object is invariably co-perceived with cognition — this is an 'apprehension of the contradictory of the pervader [of what is to be negated]': the invariable [co-perception], which contradicts the non-invariance that pervades the difference to be negated, by removing non-invariance, refutes the difference pervaded by it. One might object: if the object is not different from cognition, how does it appear as if different? Hence he says — 'it is fabricated.' As the <s>Vaināśikas</s> say —

Granted that the three <s>guṇas</s> undergo such diversity of transformation — but one transformation [is called] 'earth,' another 'water' — how can this be, since oneness would contradict the [supposed] multiplicity of the self? Anticipating this doubt, he introduces the <s>sūtra</s> — 'when all the <s>guṇas</s>' etc. The reality of a thing follows from the oneness of transformation. A single transformation of many [factors] is indeed observed — for example, the hairs of cows, horses, buffaloes, and elephants, when cast [into a brine pit], undergo a single transformation characterized by the quality of saltness; similarly, wick, oil, and fire [produce] a single [transformation as] a lamp. In this way, even though the <s>guṇas</s> are many, their transformation is one; hence each <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element), gross element, and product of elements has a single reality. For those [<s>guṇas</s>] that are apprehension-natured, being <s>sattva</s>-predominant and hence luminous in nature — being subsidiary effects of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense) — there is a single transformation in the form of an instrument of cognition: the ear as a sense organ. Of those very <s>guṇas</s>, being <s>tamas</s>-predominant and hence inert in nature, being object-natured — there is a single transformation in the form of the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s> (sound subtle-element): sound as an object. '<s>Śabda</s>' means the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s>. 'Object' indicates its inertness — not that the <s>tanmātra</s> could be an object of the ear [directly]. The rest is easy to understand. Now he raises the <s>Vijñānavādin</s> (Buddhist idealist), [specifically] the <s>Vaināśika</s> — 'there is no object associated with cognition.' For if the elements and their products were different from mere cognition, then such a <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) could be postulated as their cause of origination — but they do not exist as ultimately different from cognition. Then how can the postulation of <s>Pradhāna</s> be justified, and how can the postulation of sense organs — modifications of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> — that grasp [objects] be justified? Thus — since an inert object, being by nature non-self-luminous, there is no object associated with cognition. 'Association' means relation; its absence is 'non-association.'

children.text:
"sahopalambhaniyamād abhedo nīlataddhiyoḥ/ bhedaś ca bhrāntivijñānair dṛśya indāv
      ivādvaye" iti//
children.translated_text: "Due to the rule of co-perception, blue and the cognition of blue are non-different; their apparent difference arises from erroneous cognitions, like a visible [second moon] in the non-dual [moon]."

children.text:
kalpitatvaṃ viśadayati --- jñānaparikalpaneti/ nirākaroti --- ta iti/ te kathaṃ
      śraddheyavacanāḥ syur iti saṃbandhaḥ/ pratijñānam upasthitaṃ pratyupasthitam/ katham ---
      tatheti/ yathā yathāvabhāsata idaṃkārāspadatvena tathā tathā svayam upasthitaṃ na tu
      kalpanopakalpitaṃ vijñānaviṣayatāpannam/ svamāhātmyeneti vijñānakāraṇatvam arthasya
      darśayati/ yasmād arthena svakīyayā grāhyaśaktyā vijñānam ajani tasmād arthasya grāhakaṃ
      tad evaṃbhūtaṃ vastu katham apramāṇātmakena vikalpavijñānabalena vikalpasyāprāmāṇikatvāt
      tadbalasyāpi tadātmano+apramāṇātmakatvaṃ, tena vastusvarūpam utsṛjyopaplutaṃ kṛtvā/
      upagṛhyeti kvacid pāṭhaḥ/ tatrāpi sa evārthaḥ/ tad evāpalapantaḥ śraddhātavyavacanāḥ
      syur iti/ idam atrākūtam --- sahopalambhaniyamaś ca vedyatvaṃ ca hetū
      saṃdigdhavyatirekatayā naikāntikau/ tathā hi --- jñānākārasya bhūtabhautikāder yad etad
      bāhyatvaṃ sthūlatvaṃ ca bhāsete na te jñāne saṃbhavataḥ/ tathā hi nānādeśavyāpitā
      sthaulyaṃ vicchinnadeśatā ca bāhyatvam/ na caikavijñānasya nānādeśavyāpitā

vicchinnadeśatā copapadyate/
      taddeśatvātaddeśatvalakṣaṇaviruddhadharmasaṃsargasyaikatrāsaṃbhavāt saṃbhave vā
      trailokyasyaikatvaprasaṅgāt/ ata evāstu vijñānabheda iti cet/ hanta bhoḥ
      paramasūkṣmagocarāṇāṃ pratyayānāṃ parasparavārtānabhijñānāṃ svagocaramātrajāgarūkāṇāṃ
      kutastyo+ayaṃ sthūlāvabhāsaḥ/ na ca vikalpagocaro+abhilāpaḥ saṃsargābhāvād
      viśadapratibhāsatvāc ca/ na ca sthūlam ālocitaṃ yatas tadupādhikasya viśadatā bhavet
      tatpṛṣṭhabhāvinaḥ/ na cāvikalpavad vikalpo+api svākāramātragocaras tasya cāsthūlatvān na
      sthūlagocaro bhavitum arhati/ tasmād bāhye ca pratyaye sthūlasya bāhyasya cāsaṃbhavād
      alīkam etad āsthātavyam/ na cālīkaṃ vijñānād abhinnaṃ vijñānasya tadvat
      tucchatvaprasaṅgāt/ tathā ca vedyatvasyābhedavyāpyatvābhāvāt kuto bhedapratipakṣatvam/
      sahopalambhaniyamaś ca sadasator iva vijñānasthaulyayoḥ sator api svabhāvād vā kutaścit
      pratibandhād vopapatsyate/ tasmād anaikāntikatvād etau hetvābhāsau vikalpamātram eva
      bāhyābhāve prasuvāte/ na ca pratyakṣamāhātmyaṃ vikalpamātreṇāpodyate/ tasmāt sādhūktaṃ
      katham apramāṇātmakena vikalpajñānabaleneti/ etena pratyayatvam api
      svapnādipratyayadṛṣṭāntena nirālambanatvasādhanam apāstam/ prameyavikalpas tv
      avayavivyavasthāpanena pratyuktaḥ/ vistaras tu nyāyakaṇikāyām anusaraṇīya iti tad iha
      kṛtaṃ vistareṇeti //4.14//
children.translated_text: nor can it occupy a delimited location — because the co-occurrence of contradictory properties, namely being-in-that-location and not-being-in-that-location, is impossible in one [entity]; or, if it were possible, the entire three worlds would collapse into unity. If one says 'then let there be a multiplicity of cognitions' — well then! Cognitions directed toward the most subtle objects, each unaware of the other's domain, awake only to their own respective object — whence for them this appearance of grossness? Nor is it the object of <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction), i.e. verbal expression, because of the absence of [real] connection and because of the vividness of the appearance. Nor has a gross [object] been perceived [by cognition] such that a [subsequent cognition] conditioned by it could have vividness, being subsequent to it. Nor is <s>vikalpa</s>, like non-conceptual [perception], directed only at its own form — and since that [own form] is not gross, [<s>vikalpa</s>] cannot have a gross object. Therefore, since grossness and externality are impossible in both external [conceptual] cognition and [in cognition generally], this [idealist position] must be regarded as false. Nor is the false non-different from cognition, because cognition would then, like it, become vacuous. And since cognizability is thus not pervaded by non-difference, how can it be the counteragent of difference? The rule of co-perception, too, like [the co-perception] of existence and non-existence, or of cognition and grossness, even when both are real, can be explained by their inherent nature or by some constraining condition. Therefore, because of their inconclusiveness, these two pseudo-reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) produce nothing but mere conceptual construction regarding the non-existence of the external [world]. Nor is the authority of direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) overthrown by mere conceptual construction. Therefore it is well said: 'How can it be [overturned] by the force of conceptual cognition which lacks the nature of a valid means of knowledge?' By this, the [argument from] 'cognition-hood' too — which attempts to prove the absence of a support [for cognition] through the analogy of dream-cognition and the like — is also refuted. The inference regarding the object of knowledge (<s>prameya-vikalpa</s>), however, is answered by establishing the [existence of] parts. But the detailed [treatment] should be followed in the <s>Nyāyakaṇikā</s> — so enough with elaboration here. (4.14)

He elucidates the fabricated nature — 'fabricated by cognition' etc. He refutes [them] — 'they' etc. How could they be speakers whose words are trustworthy? — such is the connection. The object presents itself as it appears — as the locus of 'this'-awareness — standing forth by itself, not fabricated by conceptual construction, not reduced to being merely an object of cognition. 'By its own greatness' — he shows that the object is the cause of cognition. Since cognition is produced by the object through its own graspable capacity, that cognition grasps the object. How, then, can such a real entity be overturned, made as it were refuted, by the force of conceptual cognition (<s>vikalpa</s>) which has no valid-means-of-knowledge nature — since <s>vikalpa</s> is not a valid means of knowledge, the force of it also, being of that nature, lacks the nature of a valid means of knowledge — and [how can it] abandon the own-nature of the real? 'Taken up' is an alternative reading; the meaning is the same even there. Those who deny that very [reality] — how could they be speakers whose words are trustworthy? The purport here is this: both the rule of co-perception and cognizability are inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) as reasons, because they admit of doubt regarding their negative concomitance. For the externality and grossness that appear as the form of cognition's content — of the elements and their products — these are not possible in cognition [itself]. For being spread over many locations is grossness, and occupying a delimited location is externality. But a single cognition cannot be spread over many locations,

children.text: vastusāmye cittabhedāt tayor vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ //4.15//
children.translated_text: When the object is the same, due to the difference of minds, the two have separate paths. (4.15)

children.text:
tad evam utsūtraṃ bhāṣyakṛd vijñānātiriktasthāpane yuktim uktvā sautrīṃ yuktim
      avatārayati --- kutaś caitad iti/ vastusāmye cittabhedāt tayor vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ/
      yannānātve yasyaikatvaṃ tat tato+atyantaṃ bhidyate/ yathā caitrasya jñānam ekaṃ
      bhinnebhyo devadattaviṣṇumitramaitrapratyayebhyo bhidyate/ jñānanānātve 'pi cārtho na
      bhidyata iti bhavati vijñānebhyo+anyaḥ/ abhedaś cārthasya jñānabhede+api pramātQṇāṃ
      parasparapratisaṃdhānād avasīyate/ asti hi raktadviṣṭavimūḍhamadhyasthānām ekasyāṃ
      yoṣiti pratīyamānāyāṃ pratisaṃdhānaṃ yā tvayā dṛśyate saiva mayāpīti/ tasmād vastusāmye
      cittabhedāj jñānabhedāt tayor arthajñānayor vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ svarūpabhedopāyaḥ/
      sukhajñānaṃ kāntāyāṃ kāntasya, sapatnīnāṃ duḥkhajñānam/ caitrasya tu tām avindato
      mūḍhajñānaṃ viṣādaḥ/ syād etat/ ya ekasya cittena parikalpitaḥ

kāminīlakṣaṇo+arthas tenaivānyeṣām api cittam uparajyata iti sādhāraṇam upapadyata ity
      ata āha --- na cānyeti/ tathā saty ekasmin nīlajñānavati sarva eva nīlajñānavantaḥ syur
      iti/ nanv arthavādinām apy eko+arthaḥ kathaṃ sukhādibhedabhinnavijñānahetuḥ/ na hy
      avilakṣaṇāt kāraṇāt kāryabhedo yukta ity ata āha --- sāṃkhyapakṣa iti/ ekasyaiva
      bāhyasya vastunas traiguṇyapariṇāmasya trairūpyam upapannam/ evam api sarveṣām aviśeṣeṇa
      sukhaduḥkhamohātmakaṃ vijñānaṃ syād ity ata āha --- dharmādinimittāpekṣaṃ rajaḥsahitaṃ
      sattvaṃ dharmāpekṣaṃ sukhajñānaṃ janayati/ sattvam eva tu vigalitarajaskaṃ vidyāpekṣaṃ
      mādhyasthyajñānam iti/ te ca dharmādayo na sarve sarvatra puruṣe santi kiṃ tu kaścit
      kvacid ity upapannā vyavastheti/ atra kecid āhuḥ prāvādukā jñānasahabhūr evārtho
      bhogyatvāt sukhādivad iti/ etad uktaṃ bhavati --- bhavatv artho jñānād vyatiriktas
      tathāpy asau jaḍatvān na jñānam antareṇa śakyaḥ pratipattum/ jñānena tu bhāsanīyaḥ/
      tathā ca jñānasamaya evāsti nānyadā pramāṇābhāvād iti/ tad etad utsūtraṃ tāvad dūṣayati
      bhāṣyakāraḥ --- ta etayā dvāreti/ vastu khalu sarvacittasādhāraṇam
      anekakṣaṇaparamparohyamānaṃ pariṇāmātmakam anubhūyate laukikaparīkṣakaiḥ/ tac ced
      vijñānena saha bhaven nūnam evaṃvidham evaṃ ced idamaṃśasyopari ko+ayam anurodho yena so
      'pi nāpahnūyetety arthaḥ //4.15//
children.translated_text: The object has the nature of a desired woman — by that alone the minds of others too are colored, so it would be common [to all] — to this he says: 'And not another...' If that were so, when one person has knowledge of blue, all would have knowledge of blue. But [the objection]: even for the realists (<s>arthavādins</s>), a single object — how can it be the cause of cognitions differentiated by differences of pleasure and the like? For it is not reasonable that there should be differentiation of effects from an undifferentiated cause — to this he says: 'According to the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position...' Of a single external entity, which is a transformation of the three <s>guṇas</s>, the threefold nature is established. Even so, all [persons] would indifferently have cognition consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion — to this he says: '<s>Sattva</s> combined with <s>rajas</s>, dependent on <s>dharma</s> and other causes, produces pleasurable cognition; but <s>sattva</s> freed from <s>rajas</s>, dependent on knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), [produces] cognition of equanimity.' And those <s>dharmas</s> and the rest are not all present in every <s>puruṣa</s>, but some [are found] in some — thus the arrangement is established. Here some disputants say: 'The object coexists with knowledge, because it is an object of enjoyment, like pleasure and the like.' What has been said amounts to this: let the object be distinct from knowledge; nevertheless, being inert (<s>jaḍa</s>), it cannot be apprehended without knowledge. But it must be illuminated by knowledge. And so it exists only at the time of knowledge, not at other times, because of the absence of <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) [at those times]. The <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) refutes this as being contrary to the <s>sūtra</s>: 'These, through this door...' An object is indeed common to all minds, experienced as having the nature of transformation, being carried forward through a succession of many moments, by worldly examiners. If it were [identical] with cognition, it would certainly be of such a nature — if so, regarding this aspect, what is this insistence by which even that would not be denied? — this is the meaning. (4.15)

Thus, having stated a reasoning beyond the <s>sūtra</s> [text] for establishing [the existence of objects] distinct from cognition, the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) introduces the reasoning based on the <s>sūtra</s> — 'and how is this so?' etc. 'When the object is the same, due to the difference of minds, the two have separate paths.' That whose oneness [persists] amidst the multiplicity of another — that is utterly different from that other. Just as the single cognition of <s>Caitra</s> is different from the distinct cognitions of <s>Devadatta</s>, <s>Viṣṇumitra</s>, and <s>Maitra</s> — so too, even though cognitions are many, the object is not [itself] many; hence it is other than the cognitions. And the non-difference of the object despite the difference of cognitions is ascertained from the mutual recognition among the perceivers. For among those who are amorous, hostile, deluded, and indifferent, when a single woman is being perceived, there is the mutual recognition: 'the very one you see is the one I too see.' Therefore, when the object is the same, due to the difference of minds — of cognitions — the two, namely the object and the cognitions, have separate paths — different modes of being. The cognition of happiness [arises] in the lover [regarding] the beloved woman; the cognition of pain [arises] in the co-wives. But for <s>Caitra</s>, who does not obtain her, there is a cognition of delusion, namely despondency. One might object: that which is fabricated by the mind of one person

children.text: na caikacittatantraṃ vastu tad apramāṇakaṃ tadā kiṃ syāt //4.16//
children.translated_text: And an object is not dependent on a single mind; if it were unproven (<s>apramāṇaka</s>), what would it be then? (4.16)

children.text:
mā vā bhūd idaṃaṃśasyāpahnavo jñānasahabhūr evāstv arthas tatrāpy āha --- na
      caikacittatantraṃ vastu tad apramāṇakaṃ tadā kiṃ syāt/ yad dhi ghaṭagrāhi cittaṃ tad
      yadā paṭadravyavyagratayā na ghaṭe vartate/ yad vā vivekaviṣayam āsīt tad eva ca
      nirodhaṃ samāpadyate tadā ghaṭajñānasya vā vivekajñānasya vābhāvād viveko vā ghaṭo vā
      jñānabhedamātrajīvanas tannāśān naṣṭa eva syād ity āha --- ekacitteti/ kiṃ tat syān na
      syād ity arthaḥ/ saṃbadhyamānaṃ ca cittena tadvastu viveko vā ghaṭo vā kuta utpadyeta/
      niyatakāraṇānvayavyatirekānuvidhāyibhāvāni hi kāryāṇi na svakāraṇam ativartya
      kāraṇāntarād bhavitum īśate/ mā bhūd akāraṇatve teṣāṃ kādācitkatvavyāghātaḥ/ na ca
      tajjñānakāraṇatvam eva tatkāraṇatvam iti yuktam/ āśāmodakasya modakasya copayujyamānasya
      rasavīryavipākādisāmyaprasaṅgāt/ tasmāt sādhūktaṃ saṃbadhyamānaṃ vā (ca) punaś
      citteneti/ api ca yo yo+arvāgbhāgaḥ sa sarvo madhyaparabhāgavyāptaḥ/ jñānādhīne sadbhāve
      tv asyānanubhūyamānatvān madhyaparabhāgau na sta iti vyāpakābhāvād arvāgbhāgo+api na
      syād ity arthābhāvāt kuto jñānasahabhūr artha ity āha --- ye cāsyeti/ anupasthitā
      ajñātāḥ/ upasaṃharati --- tasmād iti/ sugamaṃ śeṣam //4.16//
children.translated_text: Or let there not be denial of this aspect; let the object coexist with knowledge — even so he says: 'And an object is not dependent on a single mind; if it were unproven, what would it be then?' For when the mind that apprehends a pot, being engaged with cloth-substance, is not [directed] at the pot; or when [the mind] that had <s>viveka</s> (discrimination) as its object enters <s>nirodha</s> (cessation) — then, since there is no pot-cognition or discrimination-cognition, the discrimination or the pot, living only through the difference of cognitions, would be destroyed through their destruction — thus he says: '[If dependent on] a single mind...' What would it be or would it not be? — this is the meaning. And the object being connected with the mind — discrimination or pot — from what would it arise? For effects follow the presence and absence of their determinate causes and cannot come into being from another cause bypassing their own cause. Let there not be, in the absence of causation, the contradiction of their being occasional. Nor is it reasonable that the causation of the cognition of something is itself the causation of that thing — because of the absurd consequence that an imagined sweet (<s>āśāmodaka</s>) and an actual sweet being consumed would have the same taste, potency, and post-digestive effect. Therefore it is well said: 'And again connected with the mind...' Moreover, whatever earlier part [of an object's existence] — all of that is pervaded by middle and later parts. But if its existence depends on knowledge, since it is not experienced [when not known], the middle and later parts would not exist — and from the absence of what pervades, the earlier part also would not exist — thus, from the absence of the object, how can there be an object coexisting with knowledge? — this he says: 'And those of it...' 'Unattended to' means unknown. He summarizes: 'Therefore...' The rest is easily understood. (4.16)

children.text: taduparāgāpekṣitvāc cittasya vastu jñātājñātam //4.17//
children.translated_text: An object is known or unknown to the mind depending on the coloring (<s>uparāga</s>) of the mind by it. (4.17)

children.text:
syād etad arthaś cet svatantraḥ, sa ca jaḍasvabhāva iti na kadācit prakāśeta/ prakāśane
      vā jaḍatvam apy asyāpagatam iti bhāvo 'py apagacchet/ na jātu svabhāvam apahāya bhāvo
      vartitum arhati/ na cendriyādyādheyo jaḍasvabhāvasyārthasya dharmaḥ prakāśata iti
      sāṃpratam/ arthadharmatve nīlatvādivat sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇa ity ekaḥ śāstrārtha iti
      sarva eva vidvāṃsaḥ prasajyeran na jālmaḥ kaścid asti/ na cātītānāgatayor dharmaḥ
      pratyutpanno yuktaḥ/ tasmāt svatantro+artha upalambhaviṣaya iti manorathamātram etad ity
      ata āha --- taduparāgāpekṣitvāc cittasya vastu jñātājñātam/ jaḍasvabhāvo+apy artha
      indriyapraṇāḍikayā cittam uparañjayati/ tad evaṃbhūtaṃ cittadarpaṇam
      upasaṃkrāntapratibimbā citiśaktiś cittam arthoparaktaṃ cetayamānārtham anubhavati, na tv
      arthe kiṃcit prākaṭyādikam ādhatte/ nāpy asaṃbaddhā cittena tatpratibimbasaṃkrānter
      uktatvād iti/ yady api ca sarvagatatvāc cittasya cendriyasya cāhaṃkārikasya viṣaye nāsti
      saṃbandhas tathāpi yatra śarīre vṛttimac cittaṃ tena saha saṃbandho viṣayāṇām ity
      ayaskāntamaṇikalpā ity uktam/ ayaḥsadharmakaṃ cittam iti/
      indriyapraṇāḍikayābhisaṃbandhyoparañjayanti/ ata eva cittaṃ pariṇāmīty āha --- vastuna
      iti //4.17//
children.translated_text: [The objection] might be: if the object is independent, and it is inert (<s>jaḍa</s>) by nature, then it would never be illuminated. Or if it were illuminated, its inertness would also be gone, and thus its existence too would cease — for a thing cannot exist having abandoned its own nature. Nor is it proper [to say] that the quality of illumination belongs to the inert object as bestowed by the senses and the like. If [illumination] were a property of the object, then like blueness and the like, it would be common to all <s>puruṣas</s> — there would be one teaching, and all would be wise, none ignorant. Nor is it reasonable for a present quality [to belong] to past and future [objects]. Therefore, [the notion that] an independent object is the domain of perception is mere wishful thinking — to this he says: 'An object is known or unknown to the mind depending on the coloring of the mind by it.' Even though the object is inert by nature, it colors the mind through the channel of the senses (<s>indriya-praṇāḍikā</s>). The mind, being thus like a mirror, and the power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>) — having a reflection transferred to it [the mind-mirror] — experiences the mind colored by the object as [if it were] experiencing the object, but does not impose any manifestation or the like on the object itself. Nor is [<s>citi-śakti</s>] unconnected with the mind, since the transfer of its reflection [to the mind] has been stated. And even though the mind and the sense faculty born of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> are all-pervading, there is no connection with objects in that [all-pervading sense]; rather, wherever in a body the mind has its activity, the connection of objects is with that [body] — thus it has been said to be like a magnet. The mind is like iron. Through the channel of the senses, they [the objects] color [the mind] by being connected [with it]. Hence the mind undergoes transformation — this he says: 'Of the object...' (4.17)

children.text: sadā jñātāś cittavṛttayas tatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvāt //4.18//
children.translated_text: The modifications of the mind (<s>citta-vṛttis</s>) are always known to their master, <s>Puruṣa</s>, because of [<s>Puruṣa</s>'s] unchanging nature (<s>apariṇāmitva</s>). (4.18)

children.text:
tad evaṃ cittavyatirekiṇam artham avasthāpya tebhyaḥ pariṇatidharmakebhyo vyatiriktam
      ātmānam ādarśayituṃ tadvaidharmyam apariṇāmitvam asya vaktuṃ pūrayitvā sūtraṃ paṭhati
      --- yasya tu tad eva cittaṃ viṣayas tasya --- sadā jñātāś cittavṛttayas tatprabhoḥ
      puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvāt/ kṣiptamūḍhavikṣiptaikāgratāvasthitaṃ cittam ā nirodhāt sarvadā
      puruṣeṇānubhūyate vṛttimat tat kasya hetor yataḥ puruṣo+apariṇāmī pariṇāmitve cittavat
      puruṣo+api jñātājñātaviṣayo bhavet/

jñātaviṣaya eva tv ayam/ tasmād
      apariṇāmī/ tataś ca pariṇāmibhyo+atiricyata iti/ tad etad āha --- yadi cittavad iti/
      sadā jñātatvaṃ tu manasaḥ savṛttikasya tasya yaḥ prabhuḥ svāmī bhokteti yāvat/ tasya
      prabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvam anumāpayati/ tathā cāpariṇāminas tasya puruṣasya
      pariṇāminaś cittād bheda iti bhāvaḥ //4.18//
children.translated_text: But this [<s>Puruṣa</s>] has only known objects. Therefore, [he is] unchanging. And from that, he is distinct from things that undergo transformation. This is what he says: 'If, like the mind...' The always-known-ness [applies] to the mind along with its modifications; he whose master (<s>prabhu</s>), i.e., lord, i.e., experiencer — of that master, <s>Puruṣa</s>, he infers the unchanging nature. And thus the difference of the unchanging <s>Puruṣa</s> from the transforming mind — this is the purport. (4.18)

Thus, having established the object as distinct from the mind, in order to show the self as distinct from those [objects and mind] which have the nature of transformation, and to state its dissimilarity from them — its unchanging nature — completing [the argument], he reads the <s>sūtra</s>: 'For whom that very mind is an object, of that one — the modifications of the mind are always known to their master, <s>Puruṣa</s>, because of his unchanging nature.' The mind, whether in the distracted (<s>kṣipta</s>), stupefied (<s>mūḍha</s>), scattered (<s>vikṣipta</s>), or one-pointed (<s>ekāgra</s>) state, up to <s>nirodha</s> (cessation), is always experienced by <s>Puruṣa</s> along with its modifications. For what reason? Because <s>Puruṣa</s> is unchanging (<s>apariṇāmī</s>). If [<s>Puruṣa</s>] were subject to transformation, like the mind, <s>Puruṣa</s> too would have objects that are known and unknown.

children.text: na tat svābhāsaṃ dṛśyatvāt //4.19//
children.translated_text: That [mind] is not self-illuminating (<s>svābhāsa</s>), because of its being an object of perception (<s>dṛśyatva</s>). (4.19)

children.text:
atra vaināśikam utthāpayati --- syād āśaṅketi/ ayam arthaḥ --- syād etad evaṃ yadi
      cittam ātmano viṣayaḥ syāt, api tu svaprakāśam etad viṣayābhāsaṃ pūrvacittaṃ pratītya
      samutpannaṃ tat kutaḥ puruṣasya sadājñātaviṣayatvaṃ kutastarāṃ vāpariṇāmitayā
      pariṇāminaś cittād bheda iti/ na tat svābhāsaṃ dṛśyatvāt/ bhaved etad evaṃ yadi
      svasaṃvedanaṃ cittaṃ syān na tv etad asti/ tad dhi pariṇāmitayā nīlādivad
      anubhavavyāpyaṃ yac cānubhavavyāpyaṃ na tat svābhāsaṃ bhavitum arhati svātmani
      vṛttivirodhāt/ na hi tad eva kriyā ca karmakārakaṃ ca/ na hi pākaḥ pacyate chidā vā
      chidyate/ puruṣas tv apariṇāmī nānubhavakarmeti nāsmin svayaṃprakāśatā na yujyate/
      aparādhīnaprakāśatā hy asya svayaṃprakāśatā nānubhavakarmatā/ tasmād dṛśyatvād
      darśanakarma cittaṃ na svābhāsam/ ātmaprakāśapratibimbatayaiva cittasya tadvṛttiviṣayāḥ
      prakāśanta iti bhāvaḥ/ nanu dṛśyo+agniḥ svayaṃprakāśaś ca/ na hi yathā ghaṭādayo+agninā
      vyajyanta evam agnir agnyantareṇety ata āha --- na cāgnir atreti/ kasmāt/ na hīti/ mā
      nāmāgnir agnyantarāt prakāśiṣṭa vijñānāt tu prakāśata iti na svayaṃ prakāśata iti na
      vyabhicāra ity arthaḥ/

prakāśaś cāyam iti/ ayam iti puruṣasvabhāvāt
      prakāśād vyavacchinatti, kriyārūpaḥ prakāśa iti yāvat/ etad uktaṃ bhavati --- yā yā
      kriyā sā sā sarvā kartṛkaraṇakarmasaṃbandhena dṛṣṭā/ yathā pāko dṛṣṭaś
      caitrāgnitaṇḍulasaṃbandhena yathā vā prakāśanam/ tathā ca prakāśo+api kriyeti tayāpi
      tathā bhavitavyam/ saṃbandhaś ca bhedāśrayo nābhede saṃbhavatīty arthaḥ/ kiṃ ca
      svābhāsaṃ cittam ity agrāhyam eva kasyacid iti śabdārthaḥ/ syād etat/ mā bhūd grāhyaṃ
      cittam/ na hi grahaṇasyākāraṇasyāvyāpakasya ca nivṛttau cittanivṛttir ity ata āha ---
      svabuddhīti/ buddhiś cittaṃ, pracārā vyāpārāḥ, sattvāḥ prāṇinaḥ, cittasya vṛttibhedāḥ
      krodhalobhādayaḥ svāśrayeṇa cittena svaviṣayeṇa ca saha pratyātmam anubhūyamānāś
      cittasyāgrāhyatāṃ vighaṭayantīty arthaḥ/ svabuddhipracārapratisaṃvedanam eva viśadayati
      --- kruddho 'ham iti //4.19//
children.translated_text: 'And this is illumination' and so on. By 'this' he distinguishes [this illumination] from the illumination that is the nature of <s>Puruṣa</s> — meaning, illumination that has the form of an activity. What is being said is this: every activity whatsoever is observed in connection with agent, instrument, and object. Just as cooking is observed in connection with <s>Caitra</s>, fire, and rice; or just as illuminating [is observed in such connections]. And so illumination too, being an activity, must also be like that. And connection presupposes difference and is not possible in non-difference — this is the meaning. Moreover, 'the mind is self-illuminating' — the meaning of the word [<s>kasyacit</s>] is that this is not graspable by anyone. There might be this [objection]: Let the mind not be graspable. For indeed

Here he raises the Buddhist (<s>Vaināśika</s>) objection — 'There might be a doubt' and so on. The meaning is this: This would be so if the mind were an object of the self; but [the Buddhist says] this [mind] is self-luminous, appearing as an object, and arisen dependently upon a prior mental moment — so whence the <s>Puruṣa</s>'s having an always-known object, and even less so his difference from the changing mind due to being unchanging? [Response:] That [mind] is not self-illuminating, because it is an object of perception (<s>dṛśyatva</s>). This would be the case if the mind were self-cognizing, but it is not so. For being subject to transformation, like blue and the like, it is pervaded by experience; and what is pervaded by experience cannot be self-illuminating, because of the contradiction of an activity directed at itself. For the same thing cannot be both the action and the object of the action. For cooking is not itself cooked, nor is cutting itself cut. But <s>Puruṣa</s>, being unchanging, is not the object of experience, so self-luminosity is not unjustified for him. For his self-luminosity is his being illuminated independently of anything else, not his being the object of experience. Therefore, because of being an object of perception, the mind, being the object of seeing, is not self-illuminating — the purport is that the objects of mental modifications are illuminated only as reflections of the self's light. [Objection:] But fire is an object of perception and yet self-luminous! For it is not the case that fire is revealed by another fire, as pots and the like are revealed by fire — to this he says: 'Nor is fire here' and so on. Why? 'For it is not' and so on. Let fire not be illuminated by another fire; but it is illuminated by cognition — therefore it is not self-luminous — hence there is no counter-example — this is the meaning.

children.text: ekasamaye cobhayānavadhāraṇam //4.20//
children.translated_text: And in a single moment, both cannot be ascertained. //4.20//

children.text:
ekasamaye cobhayānavadhāraṇam/ svābhāsaṃ viṣayābhāsaṃ cittam iti bruvāṇo na tāvad
      yenaiva vyāpāreṇātmānam avadhārayati tenaiva viṣayam apīti vaktum arhati/ na hy
      avilakṣaṇo vyāpāraḥ kāryabhedāya paryāptas tasmād vyāpārabhedo+aṅgīkartavyaḥ/ na ca
      vaināśikānām utpattibhedātirikto+asti vyāpāraḥ/ na caikasyā evotpatter avilakṣaṇāyāḥ
      kāryavailakṣaṇyasaṃbhavaḥ/ tasyākasmikatvaprasaṅgāt/ na caikasyotpattidvayasaṃbhavaḥ/
      tasmād arthasya ca jñānarūpasya cāvadhāraṇaṃ naikasmin samaya iti/ tad etad
      bhāṣyeṇocyate --- na caikasmin kṣaṇa iti/ tathā coktaṃ vaināśikaiḥ ---
children.translated_text: And in a single moment, both cannot be ascertained. One who asserts that the mind illuminates both itself and the object cannot say that by the very activity by which it ascertains itself, it also ascertains the object. For an undifferentiated activity is not sufficient to produce different effects; therefore a difference in activity must be accepted. And for the Buddhists (<s>Vaināśikas</s>), there is no activity other than the difference in origination. And from a single undifferentiated origination, the production of differentiated effects is not possible, for that would lead to the absurdity of causelessness. Nor is it possible for a single [entity] to have two originations. Therefore, the ascertainment of both the object and the cognition-form is not [possible] in a single

children.text: "bhūtir yeṣāṃ kriyā saiva kārakaṃ saiva cocyate" iti/
children.translated_text: "For those whose existence is itself their activity, that very [existence] is also called their instrumental cause."

children.text:
tasmād dṛśyatvam etac cittasya sadātanaṃ svābhāsatvam apanayad draṣṭāraṃ ca draṣṭur
      apariṇāmitvaṃ ca darśayatīti siddham //4.20//
children.translated_text: Therefore, this <s>dṛśyatva</s> (objecthood) of the mind, being perpetual, removes its self-illuminating nature and demonstrates both the seer and the seer's unchanging nature — thus it is established. //4.20//

children.text: cittāntaradṛśye buddhibuddher atiprasaṅgaḥ smṛtisaṃkaraś ca //4.21//
children.translated_text: If [the mind were] perceived by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognition of cognition, and a confusion of memories. //4.21//

children.text:
punar vaināaśikam utthāpayati --- syān matiḥ/ mā bhūd dṛśyatvena svasaṃvedanam/ evam
      apy ātmā na sidhyati/ svasaṃtānavartinā caramacittakṣaṇena
      svarasaniruddhasvajanakacittakṣaṇagrahaṇād ity arthaḥ/ samaṃ ca tajjñānatvenānantaraṃ
      cāvyavahitatvena samanantaraṃ tena/ cittāntaradṛśye buddhibuddher atiprasaṅgaḥ
      smṛtisaṃkaraś ca/ buddhir iti cittam ity arthaḥ/ nāgṛhītā caramā buddhiḥ
      pūrvabuddhigrahaṇasamarthā/ na hi buddhyāsaṃbaddhā pūrvabuddhir buddhā bhavitum arhati/
      na hy agṛhītadaṇḍo daṇḍinam avagantum arhati/ tasmād anavastheti/
      vijñānavedanāsaṃjñārūpasaṃskārāḥ skandhāḥ/ sāṃkhyayogādayaḥ pravādāḥ sāṃkhyāś ca yogāś
      ca ta evādayo yeṣāṃ vaiśeṣikādipravādānāṃ te sāṃkhyayogādayaḥ pravādāḥ/ sugamam
      anyat //4.21//
children.translated_text: Again he raises the Buddhist (<s>Vaināśika</s>) objection — 'There might be the view.' Let there not be self-cognition through objecthood. Even so, the self is not established. [The Buddhist argues:] Because the final mental moment within one's own continuum grasps the preceding mental moment that has ceased by its own nature — this is the meaning. And being its knowledge, it is <s>sama</s> (equal); and being immediately successive without interval, it is <s>samanantara</s> (immediately contiguous). If [the mind were] perceived by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognition of cognition, and a confusion of memories. '<s>Buddhi</s>' here means <s>citta</s> (mind). The final cognition, if not itself grasped, is not capable of grasping the prior cognition. For a prior cognition that is not connected with [another] cognition cannot be cognized.

children.text: citer apratisaṃkramāyās tadākārāpattau svabuddhisaṃvedanam //4.22//
children.translated_text: When the non-transmigrating consciousness (<s>citi</s>) assumes its form, there is the cognition of one's own <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). //4.22//

children.text:
syād etat/ yadi cittaṃ na svābhāsaṃ nāpi cittāntaravedyam ātmanāpi kathaṃ bhokṣyate
      cittam/ na khalv ātmanaḥ svayaṃprakāśasyāpy asti kācit kriyā/ na ca tām antareṇa kartā
      na cāsaṃbaddhaś cittena karmaṇā tasya bhoktātiprasaṅgād ity āśayavān pṛcchati ---

katham iti/ sūtreṇottaram āha --- citer apratisaṃkramāyās tadākārāpattau
      svabuddhisaṃvedanam/ yat tad avocad vṛttisārūpyam itaratra
children.translated_text: 'How?' and so on. He answers with the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When the non-transmigrating consciousness assumes its form, there is the cognition of one's own <s>buddhi</s>.' That which was stated — 'conformity with the modification, in the other case'

children.text: yogasūtram 1.4
children.translated_text: <s>Yogasūtra</s> 1.4

children.text:
iti tad itaḥ
      samutthitam/ citeḥ svabuddhisaṃvedanaṃ buddhes tadākārāpattau citipratibimbādhāratayā
      tadrūpatāpattau satyām/ yathā hi candramasaḥ kriyām antareṇāpi
      saṃkrāntacandrapratibimbam amalaṃ jalam acalaṃ calam ivālavālam arālam iva candramasam
      avabhāsayati evaṃ vināpi citivyāpāram upasaṃkrāntacitipratibimbaṃ cittaṃ svagatayā
      kriyayā kriyāvatīm asaṃgatām api saṃgatāṃ citiśaktim avabhāsayad bhogyabhāvam āsādayad
      bhoktṛbhāvam āpādayati tasyā iti sūtrārthaḥ/ bhāṣyam apy etad artham asakṛt tatra tatra
      vyākhyātam iti na vyākhyātam atra/ buddhivṛttyaviśiṣṭatve jñānavṛtter āgamam udāharati
      --- tathā coktaṃ --- na pātālam iti/ śāśvatasya śivasya brahmaṇo viśuddhasvabhāvasya
      citicchāyāpannāṃ manovṛttim eva citicchāyāpannatvāc citer apy aviśiṣṭāṃ guhāṃ vedayante/
      tasyām eva guhāyāṃ tad guhyaṃ brahma tadapanaye tu svayaṃprakāśam anāvaraṇam anupasargaṃ
      pradyotate caramadehasya bhagavata iti //4.22//
children.translated_text: — that arises from this [principle]. The cognition by consciousness (<s>citi</s>) of its own <s>buddhi</s> occurs when there is the assumption of its form — that is, when [the mind] attains the nature of [consciousness] by serving as the substrate for the reflection of consciousness. For just as the moon, without any action on its part, [is reflected in] pure water that has received the moon's reflection, and that still water appears as if moving, as if [it were] the moon itself, similarly, without any activity of consciousness, the mind that has received the reflection of consciousness, through its own activity, illuminates the unconnected consciousness-power as if connected, attains the status of the enjoyed, and confers the status of the enjoyer upon it — this is the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s>.

There might be this [question]: If the mind is not self-illuminating, nor cognizable by another mind, how will the mind be experienced even by the self? For even for the self, which is self-luminous, there is no activity whatsoever. And without that [activity], there is no agent; and if not connected with the mind as object, the absurdity would follow that he would be the experiencer [of everything] — with this intention, he asks —

children.text: draṣṭṛdṛśyoparaktaṃ cittaṃ sarvārtham //4.23//
children.translated_text: The mind, colored by seer and seen, [comprehends] all objects. //4.23//

children.text:
tad evaṃ dṛśyatvena cittasya pariṇāminas tadatiriktaḥ pumān apariṇatidharmopapāditaḥ
      saṃprati lokapratyakṣam apy atra pramāṇayati --- ataś caitad iti/ avaśyaṃ caitad ity
      arthaḥ/ draṣṭṛdṛśyoparaktaṃ cittaṃ sarvārtham/ yathā hi nīlādyanuraktaṃ cittaṃ
      nīlādyarthaṃ pratyakṣeṇaivāvasthāpayati evaṃ

draṣṭṛcchāyāpattyā
      tadanuraktaṃ cittaṃ draṣṭāram api pratyakṣeṇāvasthāpayati/ asti hi tryākāraṃ jñānaṃ
      nīlam ahaṃ saṃpratyemīti/ tasmāj jñeyavat tajjñātāpi pratyakṣasiddho+api na
      vivicyāvasthāpito yathā jale candramaso bimbam/ na tv etāvatā tad apratyakṣam/ na cāsya
      jalagatatve tad apramāṇam iti candrarūpe+apy apramāṇaṃ bhavitum arhati/ tasmāc
      cittapratibimbatayā caitanyagocarāpi cittavṛttir na caitanyāgocareti/ tad idaṃ
      sarvārthatvaṃ cittasyeti/ tad etad āha --- mano hīti/ na kevalaṃ tadākārāpattyā
      mantavyenārthenoparaktaṃ mano+api tu svayaṃ ceti/ cakāro bhinnakramaḥ puruṣeṇety
      asyānantaraṃ draṣṭavyaḥ/ tacchāyāpattiḥ puruṣasya vṛttiḥ/ iyaṃ ca caitanyacchāyāpattiś
      cittasya vaināśikair abhyupetavyā/ katham anyathā citte caitanyam eta āropayāṃ babhūvur
      ity āha --- tad aneneti/ kecid vaināśikā bāhyārthavādinaḥ/ apare vijñānamātravādinaḥ/
      nanu yadi cittam eva draṣṭrākāraṃ dṛśyākāraṃ cānubhūyate hanta cittād abhinnāv evāstāṃ
      draṣṭṛdṛśyau/ yathāhuḥ ---
children.translated_text: Through the reflection of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>), the mind (<s>citta</s>), colored by that [reflection], establishes even the seer through direct perception. For knowledge has a threefold form: "blue," "I," and "I am now cognizing this." Therefore, just as the knowable [object], so too the knower of it, though established through direct perception, is not discriminately ascertained — just as the reflection of the moon in water. But this does not mean it is not directly perceived. And just as the fact that [the moon's reflection] appears in water does not make it invalid as a means of knowledge regarding the actual form of the moon, so too the mental modification (<s>cittavṛtti</s>), even though it has consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) as its domain by virtue of being a reflection in the mind, is not outside the domain of consciousness. This is the omniform nature (<s>sarvārthatva</s>) of the mind. He states this thus: "For the mind" (<s>mano hi</s>). Not only is the mind colored by the object to be known through the assumption of its form, but also by itself — and the word "ca" (and) is displaced in sequence and should be read immediately after "by <s>Puruṣa</s>." The "reflection of its shadow" means the modification of <s>Puruṣa</s>. And this assumption of the reflection of consciousness by the mind must be accepted by the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (Buddhists). How else could they have superimposed consciousness upon the mind? — thus he says "by this" (<s>tad anena</s>). Some <s>Vaināśikas</s> are proponents of external objects; others are proponents of consciousness-only (<s>vijñānamātravādin</s>). But if the mind itself is experienced as having the form of the seer and the form of the seen, then let the seer and the seen be indeed non-different from the mind! As they say:

Thus, since the mind is an object of perception and subject to transformation, a <s>Puruṣa</s> (person/self) distinct from it, established through the property of non-transformation, [exists]. Now he also validates ordinary perception as a means of knowledge in this matter — 'And therefore this' and so on. 'And necessarily this' — this is the meaning. The mind, colored by seer and seen, [comprehends] all objects. For just as the mind, colored by blue and the like, establishes [the existence of] objects such as blue and the like through direct perception alone, so too

children.text:
"abhinno+api hi buddhyātmā viparyāsitadarśanaiḥ/ grāhyagrāhakasaṃvittibhedavān iva
      lakṣyate" iti//
cf. pramāṇavārttikam 3.353
children.translated_text: [Cf. <s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> 3.353]

"For the <s>buddhi</s>-self (<s>buddhyātmā</s>), though non-different, appears to those of distorted perception as if possessing the distinctions of the apprehensible (<s>grāhya</s>), the apprehender (<s>grāhaka</s>), and awareness (<s>saṃvitti</s>)."

children.text:
tat katham ete+anukampanīyā ity ata āha --- samādhiprajñāyām iti/ te khalūktābhir
      upapattibhiś cittātiriktaṃ puruṣam abhyupagamyāpy aṣṭāṅgayogopadeśena samādhiprajñāyām
      ātmagocarāyām avatārya bodhayitavyāḥ/ tadyathā --- samādhiprajñāyāṃ prajñeyo+artha ātmā
      pratibimbībhūto+anyaḥ kasmāt tasyātmana ālambanībhūtatvāt/ atha cittād abhinnam eva
      kasmān nālambanaṃ bhavatīti

yadi yuktibodhito+api vaiyātyād vadet tatra
      hetum āha --- sa ced ātmarūpo+arthaś cittamātraṃ syān na tu tato vyatiriktas tataḥ
      kathaṃ prajñayaiva prajñārūpam avadhāryeta svātmani vṛttivirodhāt/ upasaṃharati ---
      tasmād iti/ samīcīnopadeśenānukampitā bhavantīty āha --- evam iti/ jātitaḥ svabhāvata
      ity arthaḥ //4.23//
children.translated_text: If, even when instructed by reasoning, one should speak otherwise out of perversity, he states the reason: "If that object, which is of the nature of the self, were merely the mind and not distinct from it, then how could what is of the nature of cognition be determined by cognition itself? — because of the impossibility of an activity directed upon oneself." He concludes: "therefore" (<s>tasmāt</s>). That they are shown compassion through proper instruction, he says: "thus" (<s>evam</s>). "By birth, by nature" — this is the meaning. (4.23)

As to how these [Buddhists] deserve compassion, he says: "in the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>" (<s>samādhiprajñāyām</s>). They, having accepted — through the reasonings stated — a <s>Puruṣa</s> distinct from the mind, should nevertheless be guided through the instruction of the eightfold yoga (<s>aṣṭāṅgayoga</s>) and brought to the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, which has the self as its domain, so as to be enlightened. Thus: in the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, the object to be known is the self, which has become a reflection [in the mind] — it is other [than the mind]. Why? Because the self has become the object of support (<s>ālambana</s>) [for that cognition]. Now, if it were entirely non-different from the mind, why would it not be the support?

children.text: tad asaṃkhyeyavāsanābhiś citram api parārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt //4.24//
children.translated_text: That [mind], though variegated by innumerable <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), exists for the sake of another (<s>parārtha</s>), because it acts in combination (<s>saṃhatyakāritva</s>). (4.24)

children.text:
cittātiriktātmasadbhāve hetvantaram avatārayati --- kutaś ceti/ tad
      asaṃkhyeyavāsanābhiś citram api parārthaṃ saṃhatyakāritvāt/ yady apy asaṃkhyeyāḥ
      karmavāsanāḥ kleśavāsanāś ca cittam evādhiśerate na tu puruṣam/ tathā ca vāsanādhīnā
      vipākāś cittāśrayatayā cittasya bhoktṛtām āvahanti, bhoktur arthe ca bhogyam iti sarvaṃ
      cittārthaṃ prāptaṃ, tathāpi tac cittam asaṃkhyeyavāsanāvicitram api parārtham/ kasmāt/
      saṃhatyakāritvād iti sūtrārthaḥ/ vyācaṣṭe --- tad etad iti/ syād etac cittaṃ saṃhatyāpi
      kariṣyati svārthaṃ ca bhaviṣyati kaḥ khalu virodha iti yadi kaścid brūyāt taṃ pratyāha
      --- saṃhatyakāriṇeti/ sukhacittam iti bhogam upalakṣayati/ tena duḥkhacittam api
      draṣṭavyam/ jñānam ity apavarga uktaḥ/ etad uktaṃ bhavati --- sukhaduḥkhe citte
      pratikūlānukūlātmake nātmani saṃbhavataḥ/ svātmani vṛttivirodhāt/ na cānyo+api
      saṃhatyakārī sākṣāt paramparayā vā sukhaduḥkhe vidadhānas tābhyām anukūlanīyaḥ
      pratikūlanīyo vā/ tasmād yaḥ sākṣāt paramparayā vā na sukhaduḥkhayor vyāpriyate sa
      evābhyām anukūlanīyaḥ pratikūlanīyo vā/ sa ca nityodāsīnaḥ puruṣa evam

apavṛjyate yena jñānena tasyāpi jñeyatantratvāt svātmani ca vṛttivirodhān na
      jñānārthatvam/ na bāhyaviṣayād asmād apavargasaṃbhavo videhaprakṛtilayānām
      apavargāsaṃbhavāt/ tasmāt tajjñānam api puruṣārtham eva na tat svārthaṃ nāpi
      paramātrārtham/ saṃhataparārthatve cānavasthāprasaṅgād asaṃhataparārthasiddhir iti //4.24//
children.translated_text: is released by that knowledge — and since even that [liberating] knowledge is dependent on the knowable, and since an activity directed upon oneself is impossible, [the mind] cannot be the purpose of knowledge. Liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) is not possible from this external object [i.e., the mind], because liberation is impossible for the <s>videha</s>-s (disembodied ones) and <s>prakṛtilaya</s>-s (those merged in nature). Therefore, that knowledge too exists for the sake of <s>Puruṣa</s> alone — it is not for its own sake, nor for the sake of the supreme self alone. And since the acceptance of combination-for-another's-purpose leads to an infinite regress, the existence of a non-composite entity [<s>Puruṣa</s>] that exists for another's purpose is established. (4.24)

He introduces another reason for the existence of a self distinct from the mind: "And why?" (<s>kutaś ca</s>). That [mind], though variegated by innumerable <s>vāsanās</s>, exists for the sake of another, because it acts in combination. Even though innumerable <s>vāsanās</s> of <s>karma</s> and <s>vāsanās</s> of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) inhere in the mind alone and not in <s>Puruṣa</s>, and though the fruitions (<s>vipāka</s>) dependent on <s>vāsanās</s> bring about the mind's role as experiencer by virtue of being based in the mind, and though everything is thus for the mind's purpose since what is experienced exists for the experiencer — nevertheless, that mind, variegated by innumerable <s>vāsanās</s>,

children.text: viśeṣadarśina ātmabhāvabhāvanānivṛttiḥ //4.25//
children.translated_text: For one who sees the distinction (<s>viśeṣadarśin</s>), the contemplation of the nature of the self (<s>ātmabhāvabhāvanā</s>) ceases. (4.25)

children.text:
tad evaṃ kaivalyamūlabījaṃ yuktimayam ātmadarśanam uktvā tadupadeśādhikṛtaṃ puruṣam
      anadhikṛtapuruṣāntarād vyāvṛttam āha --- viśeṣadarśina ātmabhāvabhāvanānivṛttiḥ/
      yasyātmabhāve bhāvanāsti tasyāṣṭāṅgayogopadeśād anutiṣṭhato yuñjānasya tatparipākāc
      cittasattvapuruṣayor viśeṣadarśanād ātmabhāvabhāvanā nivartate/ yasyātmabhāvabhāvanaiva
      nāsti nāstikasya tasyopadeśānadhikṛtasyāpariniścitātmatatparalokabhāvasya nopadeśo na
      viśeṣadarśanaṃ nātmabhāvabhāvanānivṛttir iti sūtrārthaḥ/ nanv ātmabhāvabhāvanāyāś
      cittavartinyāḥ kuto+avagama ity ata āha --- yathā prāvṛṣīti/ prāgbhavīyaṃ
      tattvadarśanabījam apavargabhāgīyaṃ yat karmāṣṭāṅgayogānuṣṭhānaṃ tad ekadeśānuṣṭhānaṃ vā
      tadabhinirvartitam astīty anumīyate/ tasya cātmabhāvabhāvanāvaśyam eva svābhāvikī
      vastvabhyāsaṃ vināpi pravartate/ anadhikāriṇam āgamināṃ vacanena darśayati ---
      yasyābhāvād idam iti/ pūrvapakṣo nāsti karmaphalaṃ paralokino 'bhāvāt paralokābhāva iti,
      tatra rucir aruciś ca nirṇaye pañcaviṃśatitattvaviṣaye/

ātmabhāvabhāvanā
      prāg vyākhyātā/ viśeṣadarśinaḥ parāmarśam āha --- cittasyaiveti/ tasya (asya)
      viśeṣadarśanakuśalasyātmabhāvabhāvanā nivartata iti //4.25//
children.translated_text: The contemplation of the nature of the self (<s>ātmabhāvabhāvanā</s>) has been previously explained. He elaborates on "one who sees the distinction" — "of the mind itself" (<s>cittasyaiva</s>). For this one, skilled in discriminative seeing, the contemplation of the nature of the self ceases. (4.25)

Thus, having stated the rational vision of the self as the root-seed of <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation), he describes the person qualified for that instruction, distinguishing him from the unqualified — "For one who sees the distinction, the contemplation of the nature of the self ceases." For one who has contemplation about the nature of the self, through the instruction of the eightfold yoga (<s>aṣṭāṅgayoga</s>), by practicing and applying [himself], through the maturation thereof, from the discriminative vision of the distinction between the <s>sattva</s> (pure aspect) of the mind and <s>Puruṣa</s>, the contemplation of the nature of the self ceases. For one who has no contemplation of the nature of the self — the nihilist (<s>nāstika</s>), who is unqualified for instruction —

children.text: tadā vivekanimnaṃ kaivalyaprāgbhāraṃ cittam //4.26//
children.translated_text: Then the mind, inclined toward discrimination (<s>vivekanimna</s>), gravitates toward <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). (4.26)

children.text:
atha viśeṣadarśinaḥ kīdṛśaṃ cittam ity ata āha --- tadā vivekanimnaṃ kaivalyaprāgbhāraṃ
      cittam/ nigadavyākhyātam //4.26//
children.translated_text: Now, what is the mind of the one who sees the distinction like? To this he says: "Then the mind, inclined toward discrimination, gravitates toward <s>kaivalya</s>." This is explained by the text itself (<s>nigadavyākhyāta</s>). (4.26)

children.text: tacchidreṣu pratyayāntarāṇi saṃskārebhyaḥ //4.27//
children.translated_text: In the intervals of that [discriminative knowledge], other <s>pratyayas</s> (cognitions) [arise] from <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions). (4.27)

children.text:
syād etad viśeṣadarśanaṃ ced vivekaniṣṭhaṃ, na jātu cittaṃ vyutthitaṃ syāt/ dṛśyate
      cāsya bhikṣām aṭato vyutthitam ity ata āha --- tacchidreṣu pratyayāntarāṇi
      saṃskārebhyaḥ/ pratyayeti/ pratīyate yena sa pratyayaś cittasattvaṃ tasmād vivekaś
      citeḥ/ tena nimnasya jānāmīti sākṣānmokṣo vivicya darśito na jānāmīti mohas tanmūlāv
      ahaṃkāramamakārāv aham asmīti vā mameti vā darśitau/ kṣīyamāṇāni ca tāni bījāni ceti
      samāsaḥ/ pūrvasaṃskārebhyo vyutthānasaṃskārebhyaḥ //4.27//
children.translated_text: One might object: if the discriminative vision is firmly established, the mind should never arise [from that state]. But it is observed that [even such a yogin], while going for alms, arises [from that state] — to this he says: "In the intervals of that, other <s>pratyayas</s> arise from <s>saṃskāras</s>." <s>Pratyaya</s> — that by which one cognizes — is the <s>sattva</s> (pure aspect) of the mind; from that [arises] discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) of consciousness (<s>citi</s>). From that which is inclined [toward discrimination], "I know" — thus liberation is directly shown through discrimination; "I do not know" — thus is delusion; rooted in that [delusion] are egoism (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) and the sense of "mine" (<s>mamakāra</s>) — "I am" or "mine" — these are shown,

children.text: hānam eṣāṃ kleśavad uktam //4.28//
children.translated_text: The removal of these is said to be like that of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). (4.28)

children.text:
syād etat saty api vivekavijñāne vyutthānasaṃskārā yadi pratyayāntarāṇi prasuvate kas
      tarhi hānahetur eteṣāṃ yataḥ pratyayāntarāṇi na punaḥ prasuvīrann ity ata āha --- hānam
      eṣāṃ kleśavad uktam/ aparipakvavivekajñānasyākṣīyamāṇā vyutthānasaṃskārāḥ pratyayāntaraṃ
      prasuvate

na tu paripakvavivekajñānasya kṣīṇāḥ pratyayāntarāṇi prasotum
      arhanti/ yathā vivekacchidrasamutpannā api kleśā na saṃskārāntaraṃ prasuvate tat kasya
      hetos tad ete kleśā vivekajñānavahnidagdhabījabhāvā iti/ evaṃ vyutthānasaṃskārā apīti/
      atha vyutthānasaṃskārā vivekajñānasaṃskārair niroddhavyā vivekasaṃskārāś ca
      nirodhasaṃskārair nirodhasaṃskārāṇāṃ tv abāhyaviṣayatvaṃ darśitaṃ nirodhopāyaḥ prāyaś
      cintanīya ity ata āha --- jñānasaṃskārās tv iti/ paravairāgyasaṃskārā ity arthaḥ //4.28//
children.translated_text: But for one whose discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekajñāna</s>) has fully matured, the [remaining] <s>pratyayas</s> (mental modifications) cannot produce others. Just as <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) that have arisen through gaps in discrimination cannot produce further <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) — for what reason? Because these <s>kleśas</s> have had their seeds burnt by the fire of discriminative knowledge. The same applies to the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>). Now, the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence are to be suppressed by the <s>saṃskāras</s> of discriminative knowledge, and the <s>saṃskāras</s> of discrimination by the <s>saṃskāras</s> of cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). But the <s>saṃskāras</s> of cessation have been shown to have no external object — hence the means of their cessation must be carefully considered. Therefore he says — 'but the <s>saṃskāras</s> of knowledge' etc. This means: the <s>saṃskāras</s> of supreme dispassion (<s>paravairāgya</s>). (4.28)

One might object: even when discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekavijñāna</s>) exists, if the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>) give rise to other <s>pratyayas</s> (cognitions), then what is the cause of their removal, such that those other <s>pratyayas</s> would no longer arise? To this he says: "The removal of these is said to be like that of the <s>kleśas</s>." The <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence, not yet consumed by the maturation of discriminative knowledge, give rise to other <s>pratyayas</s>,

children.text: prasaṃkhyāne+apy akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ //4.29//
children.translated_text: For one who is free from self-interest even in the highest meditation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), from the constant discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) in every way, [there arises] the <s>dharmamegha</s> (cloud of <s>dharma</s>) <s>samādhi</s>. (4.29)

children.text:
tad evaṃ sūtrakāro vyutthānanirodhopāyaṃ prasaṃkhyānam uktvā prasaṃkhyānanirodhopāyam
      āha --- prasaṃkhyāne+apy akusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyāter dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ/ tataḥ
      prasaṃkhyānān na kiṃcit sarvabhāvādhiṣṭhātṛtvādi prārthayate/ pratyuta tatrāpi kliśnāti
      pariṇāmitvadoṣadarśanena viraktaḥ sarvathā vivekakhyātir eva bhavati/ etad eva vivṛṇoti
      --- tatrāpīti/ yadā vyutthānapratyayā bhaveyus tadā nāyaṃ brāhmaṇaḥ sarvathā
      vivekakhyātir yatas tasya na pratyayāntarāṇi bhavanti tataḥ sarvathā vivekakhyātir iti/
      tadāsya dharmameghaḥ samādhir bhavati/ etad uktaṃ bhavati --- prasaṃkhyāne viraktas
      tannirodham icchan dharmameghaṃ samādhim upāsīta/ tadupāsane ca sarvathā vivekakhyātir
      bhavati/ tathā ca taṃ niroddhuṃ pārayatīti //4.29//
children.translated_text: Thus the author of the <s>sūtras</s>, having stated <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (highest meditation) as the means to suppress emergence, now states the means to suppress [even] <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> — 'For one who is free from self-interest even in <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, from the constant <s>vivekakhyāti</s> in every way, the <s>dharmamegha samādhi</s>.' From that <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, he does not desire anything — not even the mastery over all states of existence and the like. On the contrary, seeing the defect of changeability even in that, he becomes dispassionate; and [there arises] <s>vivekakhyāti</s> in every way. He elaborates this — 'even in that' etc. When the <s>pratyayas</s> of emergence would arise, this one is not a sage of constant <s>vivekakhyāti</s> in every way; but since for him no other <s>pratyayas</s> arise, therefore [he has] <s>vivekakhyāti</s> in every way. Then for him the <s>dharmamegha samādhi</s> arises. What has been said amounts to this: one who is dispassionate even toward <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, desiring its cessation, should practice the <s>dharmamegha samādhi</s>. And through the practice of that, <s>vivekakhyāti</s> in every way arises. And thus [this <s>samādhi</s>] is capable of suppressing that [<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>]. (4.29)

children.text: tataḥ kleśakarmanivṛttiḥ //4.30//
children.translated_text: From that [<s>dharmamegha samādhi</s>], the cessation of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>karma</s>. (4.30)

children.text: tasya ca prayojanam āha --- tataḥ kleśakarmanivṛttiḥ/ kasmāt punar jīvann eva vidvān

vimukto bhavati/ uttaraṃ --- yasmād iti/ kleśakarmavāsaneddhaḥ kila
      karmāśayo jātyādinidānam/ na cāsati nidāne nidānī bhavitum arhati/ yathāhātra bhagavān
      akṣapādaḥ --- "vītarāgajanmādarśanāt"
children.translated_text: The answer: 'because' etc. The <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic repository), which is fueled by the <s>vāsanās</s> (impressions) of <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karma</s>, is indeed the cause of birth and the like. And in the absence of the cause, the effect cannot come into being. As the Blessed <s>Akṣapāda</s> has said here: 'From the observation of birth in one who is free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>)' —

children.text: gautamīyanyāyasūtram 3.1.25
children.translated_text: <s>Gautamīya Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.25
He states the purpose of that [<s>dharmamegha samādhi</s>] — 'From that, the cessation of <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karma</s>.' Why does the wise one become liberated even while living?

children.text: tadā sarvāvaraṇamalāpetasya jñānasyānantyāj jñeyam alpam //4.31//
children.translated_text: Then, because of the infinity of knowledge that is free from all covering impurities, what remains to be known is little. (4.31)

children.text:
athaivaṃ dharmameghe sati kīdṛśaṃ cittam ity ata āha --- tadā sarvāvaraṇamalāpetasya
      jñānasyānantyāj jñeyam alpam/ āvriyate cittasattvam ebhir ity āvaraṇāni malāḥ
      kleśakarmāṇi sarve ca ta āvaraṇamalāś ceti sarvāvaraṇamalās tebhyo+apetasya
      cittasattvasya jñānasya jñāyate+anenety anayā vyutpattyānantyād aparimeyatvāj jñeyam
      alpam/ yathā hi śaradi ghanapaṭalamuktasya caṇḍārciṣaḥ paritaḥ pradyotamānasya
      prakāśānantyāt prakāśyā ghaṭādayo+alpāḥ prakāśante, evam apagatarajastamasaś
      cittasattvasya prakāśānantyād alpaṃ prakāśyam iti/ tad etad āha --- sarvair iti/ etad
      eva vyatirekamukhena (vyatirekamukheṇa) sphorayati --- āvarakeṇa tamasābhibhūtam iti/
      kriyāśīlena rajasā pravartitam ata evodghāṭitaṃ pradeśād apanītaṃ tama ity arthaḥ/ ata
      eva sarvān dharmāñ jñeyān mehati varṣati prakāśaneneti dharmamegha ity ucyate/ nanv ayam
      astu dharmameghaḥ samādhiḥ savāsanakleśakarmāśayapraśamahetuḥ/ atha saty apy asmin
      kasmān na jāyate punar jantur ity ata āha --- yatredam uktam iti/ kāraṇasamucchedād api
      cet kāryaṃ kriyate hanta bho maṇivedhādayo 'ndhādibhyo bhaveyuḥ pratyakṣāḥ/ tathā
      cānupapannārthatāyām ābhāṇako laukika upapannārthaḥ syāt --- avidhyad

andho maṇim iti/ āvayad grathitavān/ pratyamuñcat pinaddhavān abhyapūjayat stutavān
      iti //4.31//
children.translated_text: bored the gem.' '<s>Āvayat</s>' means strung it. '<s>Pratyamuñcat</s>' means tied it on. '<s>Abhyapūjayat</s>' means praised it. (4.31)

Now, given the existence of the <s>dharmamegha</s> [<s>samādhi</s>], what is the nature of the mind? Hence he says — 'Then, because of the infinity of knowledge that is free from all covering impurities, what remains to be known is little.' That by which the <s>citta-sattva</s> (mind-substance) is covered — those coverings, those impurities, are the <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karmas</s>; all of those are covering impurities — of the <s>citta-sattva</s> that is free from all of those; 'knowledge' — that by which one knows, according to this etymology; because of the infinity, the immeasurability [of such knowledge], what remains to be known is little. Just as in autumn, when the blazing sun is released from the mass of clouds, radiating in all directions, because of the infinity of its light, the objects to be illuminated — pots and the like — appear as few, so too for the <s>citta-sattva</s> from which <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> have departed, because of the infinity of its light, what remains to be illuminated is little. That he states — 'by all' etc. He amplifies this very point through the negative formulation — 'overpowered by <s>tamas</s> which conceals' etc. Set in motion by <s>rajas</s> whose nature is activity — therefore [when <s>rajas</s>] has opened [a region] — the <s>tamas</s> is removed from that region — this is the meaning. Therefore, it rains upon, illuminates, all knowable <s>dharmas</s> — hence it is called <s>dharmamegha</s> (cloud of <s>dharma</s>). Now, let this <s>dharmamegha samādhi</s> be the cause of the cessation of <s>kleśas</s>, <s>karma</s>, and <s>karmāśaya</s> together with their <s>vāsanās</s> — but even when it exists, why is the being not born again? Hence he says — 'where this has been stated' etc. If an effect could be produced even when the cause is completely destroyed — well then! Gem-boring and the like could be accomplished even by the blind and others! And if that absurd conclusion were accepted, then this popular saying, which [normally] has a meaningful point, would [truly] apply — 'the blind man

children.text: tataḥ kṛtārthānāṃ pariṇāmakramasamāptir guṇānām //4.32//
children.translated_text: From that, for the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature) whose purpose has been fulfilled, [there is] the completion of the sequence of transformations. (4.32)

children.text:
nanu dharmameghasya parā kāṣṭhā jñānaprasādamātraṃ paraṃ vairāgyaṃ samūlaghātam
      apahantu vyutthānasamādhisaṃskārān sakleśakarmāśayān guṇās tu svata eva
      vikārakaraṇaśīlāḥ kasmāt tādṛśam api puruṣaṃ prati dehendriyādīn nārabhanta ity ata āha
      --- tataḥ kṛtārthānāṃ pariṇāmakramasamāptir guṇānām/ śīlam idaṃ guṇānāṃ yad amī yaṃ
      prati kṛtārthās taṃ prati na pravartanta iti bhāvaḥ //4.32//
children.translated_text: Now, the supreme limit of the <s>dharmamegha</s> [<s>samādhi</s>] is merely the clarity of knowledge, and supreme dispassion (<s>paraṃ vairāgya</s>) is capable of destroying, root and all, the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence and <s>samādhi</s> together with the <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karmāśayas</s>. But the <s>guṇas</s> are by their very nature inclined to produce modifications — why then do they not produce body, sense organs, and the like even for such a <s>puruṣa</s>? Hence he says — 'From that, for the <s>guṇas</s> whose purpose has been fulfilled, the completion of the sequence of transformations.' This is the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>: those with respect to whom they have fulfilled their purpose, toward those they do not operate — such is the purport. (4.32)

children.text: kṣaṇapratiyogī pariṇāmāparāntanirgrāhyaḥ kramaḥ //4.33//
children.translated_text: Sequence (<s>krama</s>) is that which correlates with moments (<s>kṣaṇas</s>) and is apprehended at the final stage of transformation. (4.33)

children.text:
atrāntare pariṇāmakramaṃ pṛcchati --- atha ko+ayam iti/ kṣaṇapratiyogī
      pariṇāmāparāntanirgrāhyaḥ kramaḥ/ pariṇāmakramaḥ kṣaṇapratiyogī kṣaṇaḥ pratisaṃbandhī
      yasya sa tathoktaḥ/ kṣaṇapracayāśraya ity arthaḥ/ na jātu kramaḥ kramavantam antareṇa
      śakyo nirūpayitum/ na caikasyaiva kṣaṇasya kramaḥ/ tasmāt kṣaṇapracayāśrayaḥ
      pariśiṣyate/ tad idam āha --- kṣaṇānantaryeti/ pariṇāmakrame pramāṇam āha ---
      pariṇāmasyeti/ navasya hi vastrasya prayatnasaṃrakṣitasyāpi cireṇa purāṇatā dṛśyate/
      so+ayaṃ pariṇāmasyāparāntaḥ paryavasānaṃ, tena hi pariṇāmasya kramaḥ/ tataḥ prāg api
      purāṇatāyāḥ sūkṣmasūkṣmatarasūkṣmatamasthūlasthūlatarasthūlatamatvādīnāṃ paurvāparyam
      anumīyate/ etad eva vyatirekamukhena (vyatirekamukheṇa) darśayati --- na hīti/
      ananubhūto+aprāptaḥ kramakṣaṇo yayā sā tathoktā/ nanv eṣa kramaḥ pradhānasya na
      saṃbhavati tasya nityatvād ity ata āha ---

nityeṣu ceti/ bahuvacanena
      sarvanityavyāpitāṃ kramasya pratijānīte/ tatra nityānāṃ prakārabhedaṃ darśayitvā
      nityavyāpitāṃ kramasyopapādayati --- dvayīti/ nanu kūṭasthaṃ svabhāvād apracyutam astu
      nityaṃ pariṇāmi sadaiva svarūpāc cyavamānaṃ kathaṃ nityam ity ata āha --- yasminn iti/
      dharmalakṣaṇāvasthānām udayavyayadharmatvaṃ dharmiṇas tu tattvād avighāta eveti/ atha
      kiṃ pariṇāmāparāntanirgrāhyatā sarvatra kramasya nety āha --- tatra guṇadharmeṣu
      buddhyādiṣv iti/ yato labdhaparyavasāno dharmāṇāṃ vināśāt pradhānasya tu pariṇāmakramo
      na labdhaparyavasānaḥ/ nanu pradhānasya dharmarūpeṇa pariṇāmād astu pariṇāmakramaḥ/
      puruṣasya tv apariṇāminaḥ kutaḥ pariṇāmakrama ity ata āha --- kūṭastheti/ tatra
      baddhānāṃ cittāvyatirekābhimānāt tatpariṇāmena pariṇāmādhyāsaḥ/ muktānāṃ cāstikriyām
      upādāyāvāstavo+api pariṇāmo mohakalpitaḥ śabdasya puraḥsaratayā tatpṛṣṭho vikalpo
      'stikriyām upādatta iti/ guṇeṣv alabdhaparyavasānaḥ pariṇāmakrama ity uktam/ tad
      asahamānaḥ pṛcchati --- atheti/ sthityeti mahāpralayāvasthāyām/ gatyeti sṛṣṭau/ etad
      uktaṃ bhavati --- yady ānantyān na pariṇāmasamāptiḥ saṃsārasya hanta bhoḥ kathaṃ
      mahāpralayasamaye sarveṣām ātmanāṃ sahasā samucchidyeta kathaṃ ca sṛṣṭyādau
      sahasotpadyeta saṃsāraḥ/ tasmād ekaikasyātmano muktikrameṇa sarveṣāṃ vimokṣād ucchedaḥ
      sarveṣāṃ saṃsārasya krameṇeti pradhānapariṇāmakramaparisamāptiḥ/ evaṃ ca pradhānasyāpy
children.translated_text: 'And in eternal things' — by the use of the plural, he asserts that <s>krama</s> (sequence) pervades all eternal things. Therein, having shown the difference of types among eternal things, he establishes the pervadingness of <s>krama</s> in eternal things — 'Of two kinds...' But [the objection]: let that which is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), not deviated from its nature, be eternal; how can that which is transforming (<s>pariṇāmi</s>), always deviating from its own form, be eternal? To this he says — 'In which...' The arising and passing away belong to the <s>dharmas</s> (properties), <s>lakṣaṇas</s> (characteristics), and <s>avasthas</s> (states), but for the <s>dharmin</s> (substance-bearer), there is no obstruction to its reality. Now, is it the case that sequence is apprehensible at the final limit of transformation everywhere or not? To this he says — 'There, in the properties of the <s>guṇas</s> such as <s>buddhi</s> and the rest...' Since the sequence of transformation of <s>dharmas</s> reaches its conclusion through the destruction of <s>dharmas</s>; but for <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), the sequence of transformation does not reach conclusion. But let there be a sequence of transformation for <s>pradhāna</s> through transformation in the form of <s>dharmas</s>; however, for <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is unchanging, whence a sequence of transformation? To this he says — 'The immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>)...' Therein, for bound [souls], through the misconception of non-difference from <s>citta</s> (mind), there is a superimposition of transformation through the transformation of <s>citta</s>. For liberated [souls], accepting the verb of existence [as conventional usage], even an unreal transformation is imagined through delusion — the conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), following the lead of the word, accepts the verb of existence. It was said that the sequence of transformation in the <s>guṇas</s> does not reach conclusion. Unable to accept this, [the objector] asks — 'Now...' 'Staying' means in the state of <s>mahāpralaya</s> (great dissolution). 'Going' means in creation. What has been said amounts to this: if due to infinity there is no completion of transformation of <s>saṃsāra</s>, alas, how would the <s>saṃsāra</s> of all selves suddenly be cut off at the time of <s>mahāpralaya</s>, and how would <s>saṃsāra</s> suddenly arise at the beginning of creation? Therefore, through the gradual liberation of each self, the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s> for all through the liberation of all would constitute the completion of the sequence of transformation of <s>pradhāna</s>. And thus for <s>pradhāna</s> too,

children.text:
anityatvaprasaṅgaḥ/ na cāpūrvasattvaprādurbhāva iṣyate yenānantyaṃ syāt/
      tathā saty anāditvavyāhateḥ sakalaśāstrārthabhaṅgaprasaṅga iti bhāvaḥ/ uttaram āha ---
      avacanīyam anuttarārham etat/ ekāntata etasyāvacanīyatāṃ darśayitum ekāntavacanīyaṃ
      praśnaṃ darśayati asti praśna iti/ sarvo jāto mariṣyatīti praśnottaram --- oṃ bho iti/
